entry.title: You Can Buy These Rare Noguchi Lamps for the First Time
entry.summary: For the Akari lamp’s 75th anniversary, the archival VB1 and VB3 are now available.
entry.content:
In 1986, artist Isamu Noguchi represented the United States at the Venice Biennale. Outside the U.S. pavilion, he installed a massive marble slide, a design originally conceived for playgrounds, which traveled by barge in pieces to arrive at the site. Inside the pavilion were stone sculptures, a twisting helix, and artworks Noguchi had been advised not to feature so prominently: Akari “light sculptures” — lights made of mulberry-bark paper and bamboo. The lamps held the aura of commercial products rather than of fine art (similar ones were available for purchase at a museum gift shop elsewhere in Venice), and the pavilion’s curator feared including them would incite a negative critical response. The lamps stayed.

For the Akari lamp’s 75th anniversary, two of the models that were shown in Venice are being produced for the first time since: the VB1 and VB3. Both are pyramids, a shape that Noguchi wrote “seems to be nature’s way.” They can be displayed two ways: anchored to the ground with stones tied to the base, or floating free. The stones are also covered in washi paper, a detail Noguchi credited to the manufacturer — “And, oh, what a beautiful thing!”

entry.title: My New Favorite Eyeliner Makes My Signature Cat-Eye So Easy
entry.summary: Urban Decay’s Liquid Stick is a nice upgrade to the drugstore eyeliner I wore for a decade — and a worthy replacement for a discontinued beloved.
entry.content:
My first foray into makeup, when I was about 12 years old, was picking out an eyeliner from the beauty aisle at Target. It was Covergirl’s Perfect Point Plus; I was drawn to the twist-up pencil formula, which seemed more approachable than liquid eyeliner, plus it came with a built-in foam smudger on the end. That dual-ended stick became my trusty companion as I embarked on a journey of learning how to best apply eyeliner to my monolid eyes: first as I smeared it along my bottom lash line to create a distinctly raccoonlike look (ah, seventh grade!), then, as I grew more confident, how to tightline and draw a sharper cat-eye flick along my upper lids. In the end, I was loyal to the Perfect Point Plus for over a decade.

I don’t use it as much these days since, as a beauty writer, I have an abundance of options at my fingertips, and experimenting with new products is part of the job. But when I first tested Urban Decay’s Liquid Stick eyeliner, which launched at the beginning of this year, I was struck with a pang of nostalgia. Liquid Stick is essentially a more luxe, grown-up version of the Perfect Point Plus, with some handy upgrades: It’s similarly dual-sided, with a twist-up gel-pencil formula on one end and a blending brush on the other.

But while the Perfect Point Plus has a round tip, the Liquid Stick is shaped with a slim, angled tip that makes it much easier to create a defined line. And the blending brush does a much better job than the Perfect Point Plus’s foam smudger, which would sometimes leave patchy streaks in its wake. The Liquid Stick’s packaging is also more secure; the caps on the Perfect Point Plus are smaller and flimsier and would often crack or fall off the pencil due to being jostled in my makeup bag, whereas I’ve never experienced any issues with the caps of the Liquid Stick.

Even better than the warm, fuzzy feelings it inspired in me, the Liquid Stick’s formula is comparable to another significant eyeliner in my life: the long-discontinued Marc Jacobs Beauty Fineliner. (I had high hopes that the Fineliner would be resurrected when Marc Jacobs relaunched its beauty line in June, only to find that the new Drawn This Way eyeliner is an entirely different beast altogether.) The Liquid Stick isn’t quite the same, but it’s the closest I’ve found to a decent replacement.

Both the Fineliner (RIP) and the Liquid Stick are gel-pencil formulas that glide smoothly along my lash line and impart a rich, deeply pigmented line. They also both have a precise, chiseled, squared-off tip, which I personally prefer over a round or pointed tip; after 15 years of trial and error, I’ve settled on an eyeliner style centered on a subtle flick at the outer corner of my eyes that diffuses softly into my lower lash line, and the angled shape allows me to create this look with ease. And since I have monolids, any eyeliner I apply to my upper lid needs to dry fast and remain utterly smudgeproof; the Liquid Stick is waterproof, sets very quickly, and promises up to 24 hours of wear. I’ve put it through its paces with sweaty dance-cardio workouts and emerged with my eye look totally intact. (Removal, however, takes zero elbow grease. I always do a double cleanse with an oil- and then a water-based cleanser — lately I’ve been pairing Ma:nyo’s Pure Cleansing Oil with Tata Harper’s Clarifying Cleanser — and emerge with everything fully dissolved.)

The one downside of the Liquid Stick is the price. At $26, it’s much more expensive than the $7.56 Perfect Point Plus for about the same amount of product. I’ve used the Liquid Stick pretty much every day for nearly two months and still have plenty of product left in the tube. However, since I only wear it on the outer corners of my eyes, it likely lasts longer for me than it will for anyone who lines their entire lid or who draws very thick lines. So I wouldn’t recommend it for someone who’s just learning how to do their eyeliner — start with Perfect Point Plus! But if, like me, you’re a seasoned eyeliner pro who wants to create smoky eyes, cat-eyes, and everything in between, I highly suggest giving the Liquid Stick a try.

entry.content:
For this week’s Don’t Dillydally, we’ve rounded up a range of newly released products we’re particularly excited about, including striped cozy slippers; a spicy, savory panettone laced with Fly by Jing chili crisp; and pretty pink frames from a Warby Parker and Rare Beauty collaboration.

Camp Snap makes easy-to-use digital cameras and video cameras we love. Now it’s taken its original Super 8–style model and made it less than half the size to fit in kids’ hands, in four bright colors. The brand has noted several times on the product page that there is very limited inventory — so if you want one, to use now or to gift for the holidays, I’d act fast.

We really like Brunch’s hotel-inspired slippers. Its latest collaboration is with California-based clothing brand Madhappy: three pairs of shearling-lined striped slip-ons in great colors.

Fishs Eddy just dropped some tableware adorned with Edward Gorey illustrations. The plates have already sold out, but you can sign up to be notified as soon as they come back — and in the meantime, here are three dancing-skeleton-adorned drinking glasses to choose from.

Here’s a very sleek western collaboration between Tecovas and Anine Bing, featuring cowboy hats, cowboy boots, and gold-hardware belts. A number of items and some sizes are already sold out, so if you like anything left, act quickly.

If you have a holiday party host to gift or houseguests coming soon, a panettone is never a bad idea — even more so if it’s an unexpected spicy and savory variation. Olivieri 1882 made this one with Fly by Jing’s chili crisp incorporated directly into the dough. Grab one now and save it; it has a 90-day shelf life before it’s opened.

Timberland’s latest collection features Snoopy and Woodstock on its classic lace-up waterproof boots, a couple of nicely faded T-shirts, a sweatshirt, a beanie, and socks.

Peak Design’s luggage is designed for cameras and other breakable equipment, with a hard polycarbonate interior and soft fabric exterior. It has just introduced three new sizes to its lighter-weight, more affordable line, including this carry-on.

Piecework makes some of our favorite puzzles, like this 1,000-piece Dining Al Fresco on Capri one featuring a Slim Aarons photograph. It comes with three boxes of Rummo pasta, pasta-themed cocktail napkins, and a conversation game with 108 questions to keep the table talking.

Beauty brands think a lot about the shades of their makeup, so it makes sense that Warby Parker would take inspiration from just that. The brand customized five of its glasses to match various colors of Rare Beauty’s Soft Pinch Liquid Blush, some with the lenses, others the frames.

Fashion designer Christopher John Rogers has created six rugs in ten colorways for the Rug Company that toe the line of graphic and organic. They feature perfectly imperfect grids and stripes and splotches in very pretty earthy tones.

The artist duo known as Pangea has made ribbon-fastened paper hats, pompom-adorned Christmas stockings, fabric Advent calendars, hand-drawn notecards, and more whimsical, playful, and colorful holiday decorations, all available at NYC-based design shop Porta.

Travel and ski brand Yardsale just came out with its warmest jacket yet: an insulated puffer with 800-fill-power down. The shell is water-resistant 100 percent dry waxed cotton, and the high neck will keep you extra protected.

entry.title: What Crystal Waters Can’t Live Without
entry.summary: “This is something I can sip on and be all right in the morning.”
entry.content:
If you’re like us, you’ve probably wondered what everyday items famous people add to their carts, like mascara or a sleep mask. We asked singer Crystal Waters — who has a show in New York City on November 19 — about the portable nebulizer, earbuds, and castor oil moisturizer she can’t live without.

I’ve been having trouble falling asleep and staying asleep. This machine emits waves and frequencies that help you sleep. Ever since I’ve been using it, I sleep through the night. You just sit it on the side of your table at the bed and plug it in — no earplugs, no earphones or anything. I’ve been using it for three months now. I found out about it by scrolling through Instagram. Now I travel with it. It’s in my bag.

I’m on the plane all the time. These actually knock out the noise, which I love. I’ve tried all the earbuds. The Apple AirPods don’t do anything. I’ve had the over-ear ones — they get too bulky to carry. When they finally came out with the little ones that just go in your ears, I tried these and I was sold. It’s also just easy to travel with. It’s in my purse.

I discovered this six months ago. I travel so much and hotel rooms are so dry. These nebulizers have the special little saline mixture that you can put into them. It really helps keep the vocal chords moisturized. I’ve heard about it for years. Singers use it. I finally went on Amazon and was like, All right, let me try one of these. This is my second one; I like this one better. Some of them come with a mask. This one has a tube you can put your lips around so I don’t have to use a big mask, especially when I have makeup on before I go onstage. The mask really messes up the makeup, so I like the little tube.

I keep a couple of these in my bag. Instead of gum, I like to have Throat Coat. It actually works with soothing your throat. I’ve tried the sprays; they kind of still dry you out. They have tea, but the tea is hard to get when you don’t have hot water. They just started making these drops a couple years ago — that I discovered, anyway. I like the lemon flavor.

Castor oil’s always been something people use for different things. I read that if you mix it with frankincense it works well on your skin, so I’ve been using it. It takes out the puffiness and it moisturizes; you wake up and your skin feels really soft. With some of the moisturizers I use, by the time I wake up in the morning, my skin feels dry again. This roll-on has been working for me. I used to use basic castor oil that came in a big glass bottle. I was scrolling, and I saw this one that has the roller-ball. It’s easy to travel with. You don’t have to get your fingers all sticky; you can just put it on your face and keep moving.

I was told when I was young that you can’t moisturize a dirty face — you have to get that top layer off your skin. This one’s not too harsh where it’s really ripping your skin off. With all the makeup I wear, this helps get it out of my pores so I can actually get the moisturizer in. I’ve been using Clarins for decades; I’ve tried all their products. This is my favorite.

Your body’s electric. It’s made to walk barefoot, but we put rubber between ourselves and the earth. This mat really makes you feel grounded, especially when I’m not able to get out in the sun and into nature. I can put it under my desk or where I’m writing, put my feet on it and feel energized. I like this one because of the size. I’ve tried the bedsheet, the bed mat — they even make hats. I felt a little crazy with the hat on; it’s too much energy going through. I like this because of its size. If I wanted to fold it up and take it with me, I could.

They are the most delicious pretzels in the whole wide world. They are just salty enough and crunchy. I don’t wanna say they fill you up, but they hold me over until I can get a real meal.

I love all New Zealand Sauvignon Blancs, but this one’s my favorite. It has that citrusy, grapefruit taste that I love, and it goes down easy. It’s not too strong — some wines can be really strong. This is something I can sip on and be all right in the morning.

When you get up, you gotta do something for yourself — meditate, do breath work and then read something either self-help or spiritual. I’ve been reading this for the last three years. When I don’t read it, I kinda fall off a little bit. It’s really talking about forgiveness, dealing with your ego and, you know, doing unto others — all the stuff you’ve heard all your life. But forgiveness is the basic part, and that we’re all one. When you attack someone else you’re actually attacking yourself.

entry.title: My Hunt for ’90s Straight-Leg Jeans
entry.summary: Every pair I owned was cropped and stopped above the ankle, which apparently — at least according to Gen Z — isn’t the move anymore.
entry.content:
A few months ago, I was digging through my jeans for a pair to finish an outfit and ran into a hard millennial truth. Every pair I owned was cropped and stopped above the ankle, which apparently — at least according to Gen Z — isn’t the move anymore. While what actually matters to me is how a pair feels on my body and I’m not quite ready to donate my old cropped wide-leg pairs just yet, I knew it was time for something different — namely, something that went past my ankles.

I plugged every silhouette keyword I could think of into search bars, and one phrase kept coming up: ’90s straight-leg. Those were the jeans I was after. A pair that would just graze the top of my loafers or fisherman sandals, elongate my legs, and look great with everything from a white T-shirt to a layered blouse. I kept an open mind on washes, brands, and price, as long as the pair looked worn in and had an easy, ’90s-cool vibe. Below are the pairs I tried in my hunt for the best straight-leg jeans inspired by (in my opinion) the best decade, with almost no ankle in sight.

First up, I tried Banana Republic’s High-Rise ’90s Straight-Leg Jeans, which sit a little higher in the waist than other pairs I tried — I would call them more of a high-rise than a mid-rise — and have a vintage feel. They’re listed as full length with a 30-inch inseam, but on my five-six frame, the hem landed closer to my ankle than I wanted and read more like a crop. Still very cute, though! The wash is a clean mid-blue, a little brighter than the other pairs I tried, and very ’90s. I wore them out to dinner and they were comfortable through the entire evening. I liked them, but the shorter hem cut my leg line off at the ankle and I missed the long look I was aiming for. They also come in a long inseam (33 inches), which is the version I’d order next time.

I really liked these. I wore Mother’s The Reifler Jeans on a Friday evening stroll around my neighborhood, and they felt like a pair I’d owned for years. The Early Blue wash is a vintage-inspired medium blue with soft fading and a little whiskering that reads natural (not cheesy). They sit at a comfortable mid-rise on me and have real length with a 33-inch inseam and no crop at all. The leg is straight with a slight kick at the hem, giving them a touch more movement than most of my other picks. The denim is 100 percent cotton with no stretch, and the style runs small, so I went up a full size.

Of all the pairs, these felt the most vintage and had a very lived-in quality to them. The jeans are made from 100 percent cotton, so there’s zero stretch. The classic blue wash is a mid-blue that’s worn in all the right places, and they’re full length with a hem that falls a little longer than the others. They fit slightly oversize, but while they’re technically mid-rise, they sat lower on me than any other pair, closer to a low-rise. I liked how roomy they felt. I wore them on a day spent at home, and while I don’t usually wear jeans around the house, these were just as comfortable as my beloved pink sweatsuit.

I loved that Madewell’s ’90s Straight Jeans have a little more room at the waist and the leg stays straight all the way down to the hem instead of tapering at the ankle. I wore them chasing my son around the playground and then straight to dinner. They were easy to move in the whole time. The wash is on the lighter side, which I liked, but my only hesitation is the distressed hole at the knee. I’ve never been much of a ripped-jeans person, but the fit was good enough that I’m willing to live with it. Plus, when I wore them to a dinner after the park, it added a little something.

[Editor’s note: The distressed pair Angela tried is no longer available, so we’ve linked to a non-distressed pair of Madewell’s ’90s Jeans.]

I’d heard great things about Gap’s Mid Rise Straight Taper Jeans and wanted to give them a try. I wore them on a Saturday full of kid wrangling, the kind of day I’d usually reserve for soft pants. With their 30.5-inch inseam, I found they fell well past my ankle, making them one of the longest pairs in my lineup, which I loved. They’re cut straight through the hip and thigh, then taper, so they look neat without veering into skinny territory. There’s no stretch, but they were still among the comfiest jeans I tested, even after a full day of chasing kids. The dark wash I chose was a welcome change from the lighter blues I’d been living in. And at $44, they’re hard to beat, especially since they come in regular, tall, and petite fits with short, regular, and long inseams (plus plenty of washes), so it’s easy to dial in exactly what you want.

I was racing out the door to get my daughter to her soccer game, so I threw these on with a T-shirt and my Labucq silver fisherman sandals, which I’m (still) wearing as often as I can before the weather turns. I’ve worn denim from Citizens of Humanity for years but had never tried its straight-leg styles. This pair is made from 100 percent regenerative cotton with no stretch at all, yet the denim was soft enough that I skipped the usual breaking-in period. They really look and feel perfectly worn in, and the fit worked well on me. The hem grazed the top of my foot, creating one long line from waist to toe. I also love the wash, a true mid-blue that lands squarely between light and dark.

I wore Dôen’s Miller Jeans to parents’ night at my kids’ school, and I went with the Coal Black wash to make them feel a little dressier than the other blues. Paired with a striped top, they looked put-together without being fussy. They’re cut straight and full length with no crop, and the hem landed right where I wanted it, just grazing below the ankle. The fit is intentionally relaxed and slouchy, and vintage details like the button fly and pointed back pockets make them look like a pair you’d luck into at a great resale shop. Dôen suggests sizing down if you want a slimmer fit, and I took my usual 26. At $298, they’re a bit of a splurge of the bunch.

entry.title: The 12 Very Best Jeans for Women
entry.summary: No stone (wash) was left unturned.
entry.content:
Shopping for jeans can be a real guessing game. When I’m on the hunt at a store and heading to the dressing room, I usually take a pair in the size I think I am, one in the next size down, and one in the next size up. Even with that approach — and as the Strategist’s denim correspondent, who’s written about why you’re probably washing your jeans too much and that not all stretch denim is bad — I can go through racks and racks of jeans before finding a pair I’m willing to buy.

That’s why I set out to make this list of the very best jeans for women. I’ve tried on many, many pairs as I’ve written and updated this post over the years, and can assure you that the ones here will join your regular rotation. To ensure that there’s a pair for everyone, I’ve talked to dozens of denim enthusiasts (of all shapes and sizes) about their favorite pairs — from slim-cut to the super-skinny and everything in between. And to make sure there was no stone (wash) left unturned, I searched our archives for still-relevant styles and reliable pairs recommended to us by stylish people. All in all, I considered more than 50 jeans while writing this guide, but narrowed those down to only the best of the best here. (And if you’re looking for something more specific, we have guides to the best jeans under $150 and .) 

Update on November 11, 2026
We checked the prices and stock of every recommendation here.

It can seem like jeans are arbitrarily assigned numbers — some are sized according to waist measurements and others by odd or even numbers. For some, that might mean being forced to choose between a big waist gap or a pair that’s slightly too tight. In this guide, I tried to feature pairs that come in a wide range of sizes. That goes for inseam lengths too. And of course, I asked denim enthusiasts to detail the fit of their favorites as much as they could.

I listed the rise measurement for each of the recommendations below (a few brands don’t include this information in their product descriptions, which is why you’ll see “no rise listed” on a couple of pairs). Jeans that have more than a ten-inch rise fall into the “high” category, according to stylist Jessica Cadmus.

Most jeans on the market now have some kind of stretch blend to make them feel more comfortable, and you’ll often see that as a percentage of elastane, spandex, or Lycra (a.k.a. trademarked spandex) on the size tag. So to judge stretchiness here, I broke it down into three categories: not stretchy, stretchy, and very stretchy. “Not stretchy” covers jeans made completely from cotton (these are going to feel stiffer when you first wear them). “Stretchy” is for pairs with one or 2 percent stretch, which will offer some more give right at the beginning of a break-in. If jeans are “very stretchy,” they’ll have over 3 percent stretch (sometimes polyester is thrown into the blend at around 5 percent stretch to keep a pair from overstretching, too).

There are times when a cowboy-esque flare will do and times when you want the sleekness of skinny jeans. Some cuts were more popular (straight leg) than others (wide leg). But I went a step further to describe the shape of every pair — whether that’s more slim-fitting, tapered, or cropped.

Ask around, and you’ll hear about how someone splurged on their B Sides or Rudy Jude jeans. Or that someone’s had the same cheap pair of Costco jeans for years. Factoring in cost per wear, an investment can make sense, but the truth is that you can get a pair of great jeans for not that much (you don’t have to spend $300). That’s all to say that affordability was a top priority — even as inflation has come for some jeans (Levi’s Wedgies are up to $110, from $98, for example) — when thinking through which jeans made the cut. Each pair below is denoted as either $ (under $150), $$ ($150 to $200), or $$$ (over $200).

Sizes and lengths: 23–39 (plus sizes here) with 26-, 28-, and 30-inch inseams | Rise: 10.85 inches | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Straight leg | Price: $

The Wedgies might be the jeans we’ve written about most — they appear all across our archives, including topping our list of the best high-waisted jeans. After wearing them myself for over a year now, I can say the fervor around the jeans is warranted. You’re getting well-made, well-fitting jeans — for less than $100. They have a straight-leg silhouette that’s as traditional as it gets, skimming right along the hips and thighs to the hem. It’s a cut that’s universally flattering and doesn’t go out of style (you won’t ever hear that it’s “on the outs,” as other cuts are).

While everyone’s body is different, I would describe mine as hourglass-shaped, which the jeans fit by embracing me through the hips. The higher waist holds me in without making me feel too held in, too. I see the Wedgies as a bridge between too-rigid and too-stretchy denim. They don’t have much stretch (they’re made from 99 percent cotton and one percent elastane), so if you’re used to non-stretch denim, you’ll find them more forgiving than a completely rigid pair. If you’re used to stretch denim, you might feel that they’re a little tight before becoming just-right — but trust me, they will.

Another part of the Wedgie’s appeal is the different inseam lengths offered (26, 28, and 30 inches) with the shortest being suitable for most petites and the longest for taller people. I’m about five-two, and I don’t have to roll up the hem on my 26-inch-inseam pair at all. And since the jeans come in a dozen different washes, you can get them in multiples — something that those who own Wedgies take great pride in doing whenever there’s a sale. (Their following includes Bird founder Jennifer Mankins, former Madewell creative director Joyce Lee, and Dianna Cohen, founder of Crown Affair.)

Sizes and lengths: 14W–24W with a 29-inch inseam | Rise: 10.5 inches | Stretch: Not stretchy | Cut: Baggier wide-leg | Price: $

I’ve heard repeatedly from my sources that Madewell’s plus-size jeans are better than those from plus-size-specific brands like Torrid and Eloquii. Madewell not only offers a size range of 14W–28W (in addition to its standard range of sizes 23 to 33), it offers many of its most popular styles in that plus-size range.

Many of Madewell’s plus-size styles are made with stretch denim, starting at one percent elastane. The amount of stretch in a pair of Madewell jeans can range from rigid (100 percent cotton) to super stretch (starting at 2 percent elastane). The more stretch, the more likely a pair of jeans will stretch out — something to keep in mind as you choose your size. The Wide-Leg Jean in Super Stretch, for example, can “stretch out after a few wears, especially around the waist,” according to our writer Dominique Pariso. Notably, Madewell carries non-stretch plus-size denim as well (it’s an almost impossible task to find non-stretch plus-size denim, so I’m impressed by this). I included the plus-size version of its Low-Slung Baggy Crop Jeans here. They’re 100 percent cotton — making the jeans conform to your body in the long term — and in a low-slung style that isn’t usually made in plus sizes (trust me, I should know, as someone who writes about denim for a living). Just remember: Madewell’s plus-size styles tend to go quickly, so if you see something you like, don’t hesitate.

*Edit note: these were so popular they sold out! Here’s another pair that are similar in performance and quality.

Sizes and lengths: 00–15 (equivalent to 22-to-32-inch waists) with 30-, 32-, 34-, 36-, and 38-inch inseams | Rise: 11.75 inches | Stretch: Not stretchy | Cut: Tapered slim straight leg | Price: $

Wrangler newly unseated Madewell in our guide to the best jeans for tall women. Available in 30-, 32-, 34-, 36-, and 38-inch inseams (the largest range of lengths of all the jeans I heard about), the Cowboy Cut Slim-Fit Jean is long enough for those five-foot-eight and taller. At $49.99, they’re a bargain to boot.

The Wranglers made their first appearance on the Strategist in 2019 when Strategist senior editor Simone Kitchens (who happens to be 5-foot-11) described the fit as “incredible and doing good things all around for my butt and my waist.” Her review of the jeans convinced at least four friends (including Earl Earl’s Laurel Pantin and editor Amanda Fitzsimons) to get their own pairs almost immediately. I myself heard about them from artist Melly Wirtes (who’s six-foot-two) around five years later. Wirtes calls the Wranglers “fairly stiff” (they’re made with 100 percent cotton in the prewashed indigo and distressed vintage washes and 2 percent spandex in the antique and bleach washes). But the rigidness of the jeans makes them more like something resembling vintage, “holding their shape and keeping everything in place.”

But even if you’re not tall, you could get them hemmed, as Strategist senior editor Winnie Yang did (for reference, at five-foot-two, she got the shortest inseam, 30 inches). Yang got them on Kitchens’s recommendation last year. Kitchens suggests going up to a size three if you’re a size two, a seven if you’re a six, etc. “Her suggestion to take one size up from your regular size is a good one,” Yang says. Usually a size two, she went with a five and “that’s probably why they’re so comfortable.” They even stood up to a “transatlantic series of flights that (unintentionally) took 20 hours,” says Yang. “I was so surprised by how not uncomfortable they were that I even pulled on the legs a bit to check if they felt like they had any elastane in them,” she tells me.

Sizes and lengths: 23–38, with 26.5-, 28.5-, 30.5-, and 32.5-inch inseams | Rise: No rise listed | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Straight-leg | Price: $

Abercrombie’s jeans have become a favorite among petites for the inseams: “short” for those who are five feet to five-foot-three and “extra-short” for those under five feet. Although the “extra-short” length is only available in sizes 25 to 30, “short” is offered in the full range of sizes 23 through 37. But beyond the petite-specific lengths, these jeans — which are straight-legged, high-waisted, and feature some stretch — are ultracomfortable. Amy Serrano, a content creator, wore them while doing “a round of high kicks with the Radio City Rockettes” and wasn’t uncomfortable in the slightest. The jeans are tailored to fit different body types, too. Photographer Lizbeth Hernandez says they are “perfect for my curvy body,” while Serrano mentions they “hug every part of my butt perfectly.”

Sizes and lengths: 22–34, with optional inseam alteration starting at 30 inches | Rise: Not listed | Stretch: Not stretchy | Cut: Tapered straight leg | Price: $

Uniqlo offers something most jean brands don’t: an online alterations service. It’s not available for every pair, but it’s optional for many, from the High-Rise Regular Jeans in the new Uniqlo U (from designers Christopher Lemaire and Sarah-Linh Tran) to the Straight Jeans that are part of the JW Anderson collaboration. Before checkout, you can select a length for the inseam (the longest being 31 inches while the shortest is 16 inches) and different stitches for the finishing (some will be free, while others come with a fee of either $5 or $10). I don’t know how many times I’ve used it in the last year, but the combination of convenience and speed (the difference between an order with alterations than an order without alterations is only a few days) makes it a very appealing option.

If you’re trying out Uniqlo’s online alterations service for the first time, consider the Straight Jeans that are part of the JW Anderson collaboration. They were the most-recommended jeans in our guide to the best jeans under $150. “I tried a 26x31, and while I might have sized down to a 25, I liked how I could wear these lower on my hips,” says senior writer Lauren Ro. And our updates coordinator Najwa Jamal likes that “they toe the line between straight- and ever so slightly barrel-legged,” especially for “the way they fit slimly through the hip and thigh.”

Sizes and lengths: 23–42 (plus-sizes here) with 27-, 29-, and 31-inch inseams | Rise: 12 inches | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Straight-leg | Price: $

In our Strategist circle, we’ve been calling the Levi’s Ribcages the “Goldilocks of jeans” since 2019. New York deputy editor Alexis Swerdloff says that “they’re just the right amount of flared.” The Ribcages have a super-high rise that gives me longer-looking legs. But the jeans don’t cut into your ribcage, as their name would suggest. Instead, they simply cinch you at the waist. Like Swerdloff, who calls them “stiff without being too constricting,” I feel these are more on the rigid side, thanks to their thicker denim.

Sizes and lengths: 24-35 with 28- (petite), 29- (short), 30.5- (regular), and 32.5- (long), and 34.5-inch (tall) inseams | Rise: 9 inches | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Looser straight leg | Price: $

Under my stewardship, there wasn’t a low-rise jean on this guide until last year. But I can’t deny that low-rise jeans are back. In fact, our junior writer (and Gen-Z correspondent) Bella Druckman is going all in on low-rise jeans now. It was a “pair of remarkably comfortable ‘low-rise ultraloose’ jeans that freed my navel for the first time in years,” she says. “And while I’m not quite ready to say good-bye to my high-rise jeans just yet — most are in storage rather than at Goodwill — I can’t remember the last time my belly button was covered in denim.” One of her favorite pairs is Gap’s Low-Rise ’90s Loose Jean. It’s a replacement for Madewell’s Perfect Vintage Wide-Leg, which “snatched my waist but left me gasping for air,” she says. By comparison, the Gap Loose Jeans have become her “party jeans, dinner-with-friends jeans, and shopping-in-Soho jeans.” Druckman’s not the only convert: Creative strategist Carrie Carrollo previously told me the same jeans are an “approachable version of a low-rise.” Her pair hits just above her hip bones but under her belly button.

Sizes and lengths: 23-37 with 25- (petite), 27- (classic), and 30-inch (tall) inseams | Rise: 11.5 inches | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Wide-leg that’s slimmer through the hip and thigh | Price: $

J.Crew’s Slim-Wide Jean is the only pair of jeans I haven’t returned in nearly a year. It’s the quintessential wide-leg — not overwhelming, but with enough volume that it couldn’t possibly be mistaken for a straight-leg. It’s the right silhouette on me: butt-hugging and thigh-skimming but not waist-gapping. As I’ve said before: I don’t have to pull them higher to my waist or suck in my midsection while wearing them. They hold me, but not in a way that’s tight or restricting in the slightest. Depending on the wash, the Slim-Wide Jeans can be anywhere between 99 percent cotton and one percent Lycra (as “black rinse” is) or a blend of 94 percent cotton, 4 percent polyester, and 2 percent spandex (or “super stretch,” available in “cobalt”). Plus, it comes with inseam options: 24-, 27-, and 30-inch inseams (petite, standard, and tall, respectively). I’m about five-two and went with the shortest inseam — this saved me a trip to my seamstress.

Sizes and lengths: 23–37 with 33- and 36-inch inseams | Rise: 10.25 inches | Stretch: Very stretchy | Cut: Bootcut | Price: $$

Bootcut and flare are often terms used interchangeably, but a true bootcut will be less flared than a flare. The bootcut is having another moment of sorts (some blame Bella Hadid), and J.Crew is making a new pair. “I was in high school the last time flared jeans roared into the Zeitgeist. Maybe you were too,” says Wall Street Journal art editor Alexandra Citrin-Safadi. “If so, know that this pair is sharper (and, blessedly, higher cut) than our shredded Mudd bell-bottoms from 2003.”

In Citrin-Safadi’s closet clean-up last year, these jeans were among the “only denim survivors.” The reason, she says, is that they’re “sexxxy, and you have to keep the three x’s if you publish this, by the way, because I mean it.” On J.Crew’s current stretch scale — which includes the 1984 rigid and the 1996 semi-stretch — this 2003 super-stretch is the stretchiest, made with 2 percent Lycra (plus a percentage of polyester that helps them snap back). “Of course, I recognize that calling the denim ‘2003 super-stretch’ is a millennial dog whistle — my compliments to the J.Crew copy team,” Citrin-Safadi says. “It totally worked on me.” Citrin-Safadi also thinks this darker blue wash, called “resin rinse” makes “them basically interchangeable with trousers.”

*Edit note: these were so popular they sold out! Here’s another pair that are similar in performance and quality.

Sizes and lengths: 23–35 with a “regular” 27-inch inseam and “short” and “long” options in addition to “petite” and “tall” (but their lengths aren’t listed) | Rise: 12 inches | Stretch: Stretchy | Cut: Bootcut | Price: $$

Nearly everywhere that sells denim has a barrel leg nowadays — Levi’s, Mother, Madewell, etc. — and it’s as established a cut as a wide leg or a straight leg. If you’ve been looking for a barrel leg and haven’t found the right one yet, Gap’s High-Rise UltraSoft Horseshoe Jeans might be everything you’ve been trying to find. “The name suggests a bow-legged cowboy dueling stance — it brings to mind that photo of John Lennon walking like that or David Bowie in those pants,” writes our contributor Sable Yong. They have a “slightly more exaggerated parentheses shape” that Yong finds flattering. At five-two, she got the regular length, which doesn’t drag in the back, and the high-rise sits lower, at more of a mid-rise. “Let me tell you: My knees have never had such luxurious personal space without enduring the humiliating flapping of truly wide wide-leg pants,” she adds.

If Gap’s Horseshoe Jeans are too barrel-y for you, here’s an honorable mention: Agolde’s Low Curve Jean. With a curved seam that falls at the ankle, these are somewhere between barrel-leg lite and extreme barrel leg (as are Citizens of Humanity’s Horseshoe). “To me, these are a cross between a barrel and a wide leg,” says Love and Other Rugs’s Lily Sullivan. “And they would absolutely make any barrel skeptics reconsider.” But the Low Curve is $238 to the Horseshoe’s $90 — I decided Gap’s gets the Best in Class distinction, as price is always top of mind for us.

Sizes and lengths: 24–33 with a 28- and 30-inch inseam | Rise: 10.25 inches | Stretch: Not stretchy | Cut: Looser straight-leg | Price: $$

“You will never, and I mean never, catch me in skinny jeans,” says writer Jo Rosenthal. “When they went away the first time, I cheered, and the next time they go away, I’ll cheer even louder.” Rosenthal’s most-worn jeans are these Levi’s Baggy Dads, which have a much wider leg than the brand’s Wedgies or Ribcages. “Everything but the waist is baggy,” she says. Rosenthal got a size bigger than her usual, and while there wasn’t a noticeable difference in the waist measurement, they were a little bit wider in the leg that way. The Baggy Dads are loose through the hips and thighs, and are meant to stack at the ankles. While they aren’t stretchy at all, the jeans have “that Levi’s worn-in” feel from the beginning, Rosenthal tells me. Now, she’s up to three pairs. “These are like a good alibi — reliable and they never let you down,” she says. Brand consultant Katie Stone similarly owns multiple pairs: She bought her oldest pair over two years ago and her newest pair more than three months ago. Like Rosenthal, Stone finds them incredibly comfortable. “They feel like home to me,” she tells me. “I don’t even consider having them on as ‘wearing jeans’; they’re in a different category of their own.” Stone also notes that the darker washes “fit a bit tighter around the butt and hold their shape better” than the lighter ones.

Sizes and lengths: 23–34 with 30- and 32-inch inseams | Rise: 11.125 inches | Stretch: Not stretchy | Cut: Straight-leg | Price: $

You can’t go wrong with 501s if you’re looking for a jean without any stretch. It’s the legendary fit that literally started it all for Levi’s. Several people I talked to not only have old 501s, but they judge other jeans against them. “Levi’s never fails — they just get jeans and always have,” says musician AJ Michalka. “They are the jeans you can actually wear all day,” says blogger Gabrielle Arruda. Arruda mentions paying attention to the wash, as the darker shades seem to have “a slightly tighter weave, so they don’t naturally stretch out as well.” And those on the shorter side might go for the cropped 501s. “Turns out new 501s are just as good as (or at least easier and more affordable to source than) vintage 501s,” according to Ro. “They just about look like the Platonic ideal of blue jeans, because, well, they are.” That said, these do need some breaking in, as they’re non-stretch. Stylist Karla Welch used to sit in a bathtub with the jeans on to get them to fit as a teen. Her advice: “Wearing them, and wearing them, and wearing them, and wearing them.”

(For some more non-stretch denim: The Feel Studio, founded by stylist Stevie Dance, a devout Levi’s wearer, has the Genuine Jean that’s inspired by old 501s, according to Kitchens. Dancer Eva Alt calls them the jeans “you always hope to find at a vintage store — just without the work.” )

entry.title: The Best Holiday Gifts for College Students, According to Our Gen-Z Expert
entry.summary: Including all the viral squishies, blankets, and water bottles of the moment.
entry.content:
College campuses are a pressure cooker for trendy products. That means the hottest water bottle last year (Owala) has already surrendered market share to other contenders (namely, HydroJug). Some products that I didn’t foresee being buzzy with the college set — such as weighted stuffed animals and butter-shaped squishies — are at the top of everyone’s lists. So if you’re perplexed by the products on the Giftful list you just got a link to or simply don’t know where to start, there’s no need to fret. As the Strategist’s Gen-Z correspondent, I stay on top of all the most relevant tidbits, trends, and products taking over teen and 20-something wish lists. I’ve compiled everything I learned about while chatting with college students into a definitive list of Christmas gifts that won’t feel “so 2025.” I’ve organized everything by category for easy perusing.

Perhaps above all else, college students are unified by their hatred of the dorm “Big Light,” which is often large, fluorescent, and reminiscent of what you’d find in, say, an office or hospital. A sunset lamp is a softer alternative they can use at any time of day.

LED strip lights are another alternative that’s especially popular with the boys. This one comes with a remote that adjusts brightness and has up to 17 different light colors.

Waiting on line for photo booths has become a popular weekend activity for college students on urban campuses. But even if they’re just holding onto a photo-booth shot they took at a sorority date party, this frame will display the photo strip and hold some keys, too.

Manic Cherry’s skateboard-style wall art has been on the up and up when it comes to dorm-room décor. Norah Hogan, a freshman at Penn State, says the sets with leopard print and designer-brand names are especially trendy.

Forget cup ramen — all the college students are eating microwavable cups of mac and cheese. They’ve replaced Annie’s mac and cheese with Goodles’ white-cheddar shells.

Forget the Stanleys and Owalas — it’s the HydroJug that’s topping wish lists this year. The spillproof tumbler comes in several trendy patterns, like camouflage and leopard print, along with tons of solid colors.

A shaker bottle is a fail-safe gift for the guy who spends more time at the university gym than the library. Our fitness writer Brenley Goertzen says this one breaks up all the chunky bits in her shakes.

For the student whose roommate watches TikToks on full volume or loses all concept of volume while FaceTiming friends, I recommend some sleep earplugs. They’re our sleep writer’s favorite pair.

Jason Lagos, a student at Trevecca Nazarene University, says, “I like to moisturize to just give better projection and better longevity to my fragrance.” Like several students I’ve interviewed, he’s a fan of this lotion from Eos, which is experiencing a resurgence thanks to Gen Z.

Doing laundry at college can feel like a humiliation ritual where overflowing lint traps and leaky washing machines are a given. Some ridiculously indulgent detergent that smells like bergamot and vanilla can make the whole process slightly better. (Some college students recommend combining it with, say, unscented Tide or Arm & Hammer to make the bottle last longer.)

Roller Rabbit pajamas are so common on college campuses that University of Alabama student Emma Lipkin told me she and the rest of the “Crimson Tide” cheerleaders have matching pairs. So if the college student you’re shopping for already has a pair (or five), I recommend getting them an accessory with Roller Rabbit’s signature monkey pattern, like this makeup bag or a sleep mask.

Robes are a cliché gift, but college students are one of the few groups that don’t usually already have one. So if they’ve been shimmying through the hallway in a towel, get them a soft, absorbent robe. (And if they have a $10 robe from Target, replace it with this one, which is our very favorite.)

In case you missed the memo: Rainbow flip-flops were the shoe of the summer for anyone under the age of 24, and I’d expect them to be popular again next year. It might seem out of season to buy a pair in December, but it’s the custom to break these in as soon as possible.

When guys aren’t wearing Rainbow flip-flops, they’re usually wearing Birkenstock Boston clogs.

If you’re shopping for a young woman, the odds that there’s a Parke sweatshirt on her list are high. Parke’s stock can be limited and its drops are difficult to navigate, so I recommend going for a fleece from Dairy Boy instead. It’s yet another influencer-founded brand that Gen-Z girls love, but the inventory is more reliable.

The Great Sweatshirt Race is less competitive for guys. Just get them this hoodie from Abercrombie, which is available in tons of colors and sizes XS through XXXL. (I’ve heard girls like them too.)

Here’s a garment bag that doubles as a duffel, so their Princess Polly dresses and Lululemon ABC pants won’t be wrinkly when they get to their friend’s tailgate.

Yet another blast from the past: Wired earbuds are also back, according to Gen Z. I tried several colorful pairs and preferred these, which take plain old white earbuds and dress them up with hand-wrapped thread. (Though those original white ones work, too.)

Last year, the mirrored version of the Octobuddy earned a spot in our print gift guide, but I’ve just noticed it catching on with the college set in recent months.

In the last year or so, more and more college students have told me they’re coveting Hatch’s sunrise alarm clock, which simulates the light of a sunrise to signal to your body that it’s time to wake up. “Having a roommate with a really annoying alarm is frustrating, and this wakes you up so calmly and gently,” says Lucy Harris, a student at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. “If my roommate had this alarm going off, I would not be mad.”

If their late-night library sessions aren’t fueled by Celsius or Red Bull, college students are sipping (or chugging) coffee. “Having a little Nespresso machine with ice, milk, and then some of those little syrups keeps me from spending too much money,” says former Harvard student Abigail Mack.

A portable speaker is crucial to the group hang. Any speaker that fits in a backpack will do, but I hear about the JBL Clip the most often. (I’m predicting the pink and camouflage colorways will be most popular this year.)

Adjustable dumbbells are ideal for the student who got stuck with a small dorm room. These are available in several weight ranges, so you can buy one that’s best suited for the student’s strength.

“When it’s a nice day, it’s really popular to play Spikeball,” says Sean Fleck, a student at the University of Colorado Boulder. This set has three balls just in case a couple (inevitably) get lost.

Given Gen Z’s infatuation with butter yellow, it was only a matter of time before the craze hit the fidget market. These TikTok-famous butter squishies would make a nice stocking stuffer.

In the last six months, I’ve seen college students bedazzle everything from their student IDs and Halloween costumes to Sonny Angels and shotskis. This is one of the most popular bedazzling kits on Giftful, teens’ favorite wish-list-making app.

It’s become increasingly popular for college students to customize their Guess Who? games with photos of celebrities and people they know. WS Game Company makes a book-inspired version that will look nice on a shelf, but the original game works too.

Coco Wyo’s coloring books are popular among Gen-Z homebodies. The brand just released a planner, which has essentials like monthly and weekly spreads along with some coloring pages.

entry.title: On My Mind: A Christmas-Party Psychosis
entry.summary: I’m planning my annual holiday party. It’s a wild time.
entry.content:
My Strategist Brain comes due every November, so I think it’ll be my tradition to discuss my annual holiday party. After all, it does take up a lot of my brain this time of year. Three days ago, I was talking through a few decorating upgrades I’d like to make — stringing garlands and lights on the foyer ceiling, mostly — with my best friend Tiff and how it might be a challenge because I’m working through a tough health condition that makes me dizzy (more on that later). The thing is, I explained, “I have to do everything myself because people don’t have the right visual sensibilities.” The response: “You’re sounding so psychotic right now.” Tiff’s right, of course. We had just talked about how I would take it easy this year: decorate with things I can place rather than hang, not go fully neurotic about spacing and angles. But I am in party psychosis. As such, there’s an enchanted-Christmas-forest ceiling-scape with irregularly spaced pine cones, greenery sprigs, and string lights draped at 60-to-30-degree angles living in my head. I might not — probably won’t — be able to translate these thoughts into real life this year. But a host can dream. And plan. And maybe even try.

These fall into the acceptable category, according to Tiff. I can easily hang them from hooks in my windows. One thing I learned from last year was that I am generally too focused on having all my greenery be natural. That’s driven by the fact that I’m a Real Tree Truther. But after experiencing the weight of a real wreath last year and how deadly difficult it is to hang (if you’re doing so from a wall and don’t want the hook to show), I don’t think all the greens need to be real pine. I like the deep red ribbon on these too.

Stockings are also in the easy decorating category. I love the rich emerald of these. One hiccup — my New York apartment does not have a fireplace, so I’m not sure where to hang them. Any suggestions?

One more in the chill category: a not-that-Christmasy table runner.

Okay, that being said, I will have at least one real wreath, and I always get my greenery from Farmgirl Flowers. It’s great for a few reasons. First, the wreath I got last year lasted almost a month, even in the dry heat of my radiator-heated apartment. As it dried out, it still looked beautiful because it had an assortment of greens, including eucalyptus, that naturally look nice dried. And the company is reliable. Party Crystal gets really serious about timetables and deliveries, and Farmgirl hasn’t failed me yet.

I may splurge on one bouquet for the food table as well. This one says holiday without going too far, and I love peonies. I get the rest of my flowers from Trader Joe’s and arrange them the morning of the party.

On the ceiling, I like these faux cedar garlands from Joss & Main. As I said about the wreath earlier, real evergreen needles and greenery are very heavy. (I hung a real pine garland over a doorway last year and almost lost it.) The feathery look of this works with my enchanted forest idea too.

Why did it take me so long to learn of these angels? I think the reason I’m always so focused on the decorations is that they’re the things that last. The party itself, I really don’t remember. Open door, hang coat, direct guest to bar. Refresh food table, collect dirty dishes, wash if necessary. Hosting means not really enjoying the event. It’s a fugue state, really. But I poked around for help this year and found this service that sends a person to take on some of these tasks. I didn’t know you could hire a person to just … help. The booking process is pretty easy: Just be ready with the details of your event and what things you’ll need assistance with. Pricing starts at $65 per hour, which is reasonable compared with other services or hiring on your own. I’ll report back on how it works out. I’m optimistic about being able to store memories of the party this year.

I’m not really a person who relaxes, meaning my relaxation time is spent either sleeping or reading. But with my new health condition, stress and visual strain exacerbate the dizziness, so relaxation has taken on newfound importance.

These disposable heated masks are saving me. I have pretty severe eye strain. These ease that in a few minutes and help me get on with things a little faster. The warmth is just the right temperature.

I was sent this bath foam, and my new chilling-is-important attitude made me actually try it. It’s expensive, so I’m flagging here more as a potential gift for that fancy mom or aunt who is really into her soaks. The lather is extremely rich, and the floral fragrance is beautiful but unassuming and lingers on both your skin and (lightly) on your sheets.

Lastly, sleep is a priority right now, so I’m trying this book that uses cognitive behavioral therapy to improve it. I actually saw it recommended by one of our readers in the comments of a Strategist story.

entry.title: The 9 Best Women’s Raincoats
entry.summary: For drizzle or downpours.
entry.content:
Alongside a windproof umbrella and your favorite pair of rain boots, a great raincoat will help you brave the elements and look good doing it. It’s an essential item to own, whether you’re encountering the occasional drizzly day or jumping over puddles for half of the year. And if you live in New York, as I do, you know that unexpected tropical rainstorms are a given throughout spring and summer. It helps to be prepared.

To find the best raincoats for women, I spoke with outerwear experts and stylish folks about their favorite women’s raincoats, then tried out their recommendations myself. Below, find nostalgic anoraks, hardshell hiking jackets, and everything in between. While you’re here, I’ve also written guides to the best women’s parkas and rain boots.

Updated on November 11, 2026
I refreshed this list for winter 2026, adding a stylish and surprisingly inexpensive trench coat from Quince alongside a waterproof Aritzia puffer jacket.

In order to be 100 percent waterproof (as opposed to just water-resistant), a raincoat must be constructed from an impenetrable material like vinyl, plastic, or rubber. This style of raincoat is perfectly appropriate for city commutes, but not so much hiking or other athletic activities. For those, I looked for lightweight and packable jackets treated with a durable water-resistant (DWR) coating. A water-resistant jacket should keep you dry in all but the most extreme cases, and it will pack down and breathe much better than a traditional rubber coat.

Up until recently, most DWR garments made use of polyfluoroalkyl substances, otherwise known as PFAS (or, interchangeably, PFCs). PFAS break down very slowly, which is why you’ll hear them referred to as “forever” chemicals that are difficult to remove from natural ecosystems. They’re increasingly thought to harm both humans and animals, so many outdoor companies have taken the active step of replacing them with less harmful but similarly effective water-resistant tech, especially in light of recent and upcoming PFAS bans in 11 states. None of the raincoats listed here are made with PFAS.

For extra protection against the elements, I favored raincoats featuring reinforced seams, elasticized or velcro wrist cuffs, and covered zippers. For more information about the ins and outs of waterproofing, Strategist associate editor Jeremy Rellosa has written an extensive explainer on the topic.

Because your raincoat should keep you comfortable as well as dry, I looked for options with lots of (preferably zippered) pockets, underarm ventilation, and adjustable hoods. Eric Goodwin, outerwear designer and founder of Lathley, advised us to avoid insulated rain jackets for more versatility. “You can always add warm layers underneath your rain jacket,” he points out, “but if it’s a warm rainy day, you can’t take away the insulation built into the jacket.”

I sought out a range of coats, jackets, anoraks and ponchos in varying lengths and weights, from classy trench coats to hard shells with stormproof hoods. The raincoat you choose will depend on its intended use: A mid-length, mid-weight jacket is ideal for dashing between subway stations, but when hiking, you probably just want something lightweight and breathable.

Water resistance: Waterproof shell, welded seams | Comfort: Two pockets, underarm ventilation, drawstring hood | Weight and length: Mid-length, mid-weight

Stutterheim’s very Scandinavian raincoats are constructed from cotton that has been coated in a thick layer of synthetic rubber. Sleek and unusually waterproof, they simply don’t allow rain to penetrate. Water beads against the jacket’s rubbery surface and can be wiped away with the swish of a hand as though it was never there. The brand makes several styles of waterproof jackets, but after spending the past three winters trying them all out, I think this lightweight option is the best for most people. It can be folded or rolled up for travel, and drapes and swishes against the body rather than hanging more stiffly. But the brand’s original heavyweight Stockholm is also great and comes in a full-body-length version for serious storms. Size down, especially if your arms are on the shorter side.

Water resistance: Waterproof shell, welded seams | Comfort: Two pockets, underarm ventilation, drawstring hood | Weight and length: Short length, light-weight 

Danish brand Rains has become ubiquitous on water-slicked city streets in recent years, and for good reason. It makes some of the most aesthetically pleasing raincoats around, and they’re more affordable than Stutterheim’s, despite being similarly waterproof. Having worn both, I’ve found that Rains jackets are far thinner and swishier in fit. Some more subtle design differences include a shorter length, hidden snap buttons, and colored drawstrings. China-manufactured Rains jackets are completely synthetic, whereas European-manufactured Stutterheims are constructed from waterproof cotton. The standard Rains jacket has the best everyday length, but I also like the A-line and poncho versions.

Water resistance: DWR triple shell, reinforced zippers, Velcro cuffs | Comfort: Two pockets, underarm ventilation, adjustable hood | Weight and length: Short length, mid-weight, packable

I travel and hike a lot, and this Arc’teryx jacket is the first thing I pack in my suitcase or backpack every time. Yes, $500 is a lot of money to spend, but this thing weighs practically nothing and can be scrunched down and stored very easily; I recently stuffed it into my Baggu crescent bag for a Chappell Roan show at Forrest Hills and still had enough space for my wallet, phone, and a couple of merch-store purchases. It is exceptionally waterproof yet never stifling or sweaty; the fabric has a uniquely light and crisp feel. Strategist senior writer Lauren Ro recently acquired one and raved to me about how it kept her perfectly dry on deck during a particularly rainy Alaskan cruise. The fit is rather slim, so size up if you know you’ll be wearing several layers.

Water resistance: DWR nylon | Comfort: Elastic cuffs, zippered pocket, adjustable hood | Weight and length: Short length, lightweight

Way cheaper than Arctery’x and often on sale, this Patagonia jacket is literally designed to be as packable as possible, making it an ideal choice for frequent travelers, hikers, and backpackers. You could even keep it stashed away in your everyday tote. Camilla Cho, SVP of e-commerce at Vox Media, owns two Houdinis and says the fabric is “so light that you forget you have it on” yet still forms a solid barrier against rain. She likes how it packs into its own pocket and can be tossed into any bag, and adds that it is “perfect for exercising outdoors when it’s a bit breezy.”

Water resistance: Waterproof shell | Comfort: Snap cuffs, removable hood | Weight and length: Long length, light-weight 

I first heard about this coat from a Strategist reader based in rainy Portland, who told me that she, alongside “nearly a dozen” friends and family members of all shapes and sizes, are happy wearers. I simply had to try one out for myself, and found the style to be lightweight and swishy yet highly protective. Its dual-length hem (shorter at the front, longer at the back) is flattering and make wearing this coat feel like less of an imposition — sometimes the silhouettes of the Stutterheim and Rains jackets above can be a little blocky. I also recommend this coat to anyone who hates the feeling of their raincoat hood slipping off all the time, as it comes with an adjustable buckle that keeps things more secure than a drawstring. To complete the look, Ilse Jacobsen also makes a great pair of rain boots.

Water resistance: DWR polyester, sealed seams | Comfort: Two-way zipper, storm flap, closed cuffs | Weight and length: Long length, lightweight 

When Strategist contributing Nicole Prince went hunting for a stylish, non-gorpy raincoat, she was surprised by how much she liked this sub-$100, highly water-resistant trench from Quince. It is long enough to keep your pants dry, and the internal bungee cords “create an hourglass shape that feeels feminine and fashion-y without trying too hard,” she says. “The pockets are slanted, which makes it a cinch to slip your hands into, but what really makes this coat stand apart is how lightweight it is, without feeling cheap.” This coat has a swishy yet substantial feel and will keep you much drier than a standard cotton trench.

Water resistance: Water-resistant waxed-cotton shell | Comfort: Cotton lining, handwarmer pockets, optional hood | Weight and length: Short length, mid-weight

With heritage designs favored by Succession characters and British royals, Barbour’s waxed-cotton jackets have a unique texture that’s shinier than Finisterre’s, above. While these classic olive-green coats aren’t as waterproof as, say, Arctery’x’s , Goodwin notes, “They can definitely stand up to light rain,” and they’ll last forever, developing an attractive patina over time. Plus, “you can rewax them yourself if they start to lose their water resistance.” The Beadnell linked above is designed for women, but when I interviewed rewaxing experts about how to buy a Barbour, many of them said that the baggier men’s Bedale style actually works well for any gender. Unfortunately, you will have to separately purchase the brand’s hood for optimum rain protection — but the extra $55 is well worth it.

Water resistance: Water-resistant polyurethane shell | Comfort: Thumbholes, lined pockets, cinchable hood, adjustable fit | Weight and length: Heavy weight, short length

The problem with most down jackets is that they aren’t particularly waterproof and will lose their insulating powers as soon as they get wet. Not so with Aritzia’s water-repellent Rainstop puffer, which Prince also tested out during her stylish raincoat search. This jacket is “incredible,” she says. “With fabric sourced from a Japanese mill that specializes in performance fabrics, the coat is matte and exceptionally soft. The premium down kept me incredibly warm while watching two of my kids’ lacrosse games in a downpour recently, but more importantly, it kept me dry.” The brand says it’s engineered to keep you warm in temperatures up to minus-22-degrees Fahrenheit, and seams are sealed to keep water out. Prince tested the short version of this jacket, but I’ve linked the mid-length one that’ll provide more coverage.

Water resistance: Waterproof shell, reinforced seams | PFAS: PFAS-free | Comfort: Heat-reflecting | Weight and length: Mid-length, lightweight

If you’re happy to lean into the Maid of the Mist look, this affordable and reusable poncho is a “lifesaver” according to Matt Young, the head of marketing and e-commerce at Brooklyn-based outdoors store Hatchet Outdoor Supply Co. Weighing just 2.7 ounces, the waterproof, wind-resistant, and heat-reflective poncho can be packed up compactly enough to fit in your pocket, he says. “It’s ideal for unexpected downpours, rainy hikes, outdoor events — and serves as a warm and dry shelter in emergencies.” Plus, unlike plastic or polyester, the material is tear-resistant and quiet, so the poncho won’t rip or rustle while you walk.
