entry.title: How to Host Overnight Guests When You Don’t Have a Guest Room
entry.summary: Make your friends and family feel welcome and comfortable, even if you live in a one-bedroom apartment.
entry.content:
Until recently, my partner and I lived in a one-bedroom apartment that was just under 700 square feet. Most of the time, it was really all the space we needed for two people. But every so often, a friend or family member came to visit, and suddenly I was scrambling to make my living room feel like an adequate place for a guest to sleep.

Of course, I certainly wasn’t the first person, or the last, who didn’t have a room sitting empty, just waiting for guests to arrive. I also didn’t have an office or a finished basement or any other “extra” space that could temporarily serve as a guest room. So for my fellow small-home dwellers, I spoke to three experts on hosting and interior design in small spaces to find out how to be the best host possible in a home the size of a shoe box.

Not only did they give me some great tips about how to set up my home for visitors (spoiler: I’m about to buy a luggage rack, and I’m now convinced my next couch should be a sleeper sofa), they also shared plenty of cheap or free things that hosts can do to make their guests comfortable. By stepping into your guests’ shoes, you can preemptively try to avoid any situations that may feel frustrating or awkward. Just showing you considered their needs will go a long way; read on for a play-by-play of what to think about before they arrive.

Updated on November 11, 2026
All these small-space picks have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

The first question, naturally, is “Where will they sleep?” The main options are usually an air mattress or a piece of furniture that doubles as a bed, whether that’s a sleeper sofa, a daybed, a trundle, a futon, or a Murphy bed.

If new furniture isn’t in your budget — or you simply don’t have the time or desire to redecorate your living room — a trusty air mattress (or air-mattress alternative) will get the job done. Interior designer Shamika Lynch from Maximizing Tiny advises picking a taller model, around 18 inches high, so your guests will feel more like they are sleeping on a “real” bed. She also recommends setting it up on a cushioned surface if possible. “A good rug with a nice tuft or with a rug pad underneath is good to have in your living room anyway,” Lynch says. And as long as you have the floor space, spring for a full or queen size — that way you can accommodate single people, couples, kids, or any other guests who come your way. This is our favorite air mattress, and it comes in an extra-tall 20-inch height. When I tested it, I was impressed by how high it sits off the floor; the height makes it feel much more dignified to sleep on, plus it’s much easier to get onto and off of. It has an internal pump, so all you have to do is plug it in, twist open the valve, and flip a switch to inflate it.

“If you are in one of those spaces where you’re not going to materialize any space overnight, your choices in your furniture selections are key,” says Kaelyn Guerin of interior-design company Haus Guerin. For her, the key is a good sleeper sofa; compared to an air mattress, it will be a big jump up in comfort for your guests, plus it can be a more integral part of your living space as an everyday couch. (She prefers a sleeper sofa over a Murphy bed for this reason, since Murphy beds take up a lot of wall space but typically aren’t as functional when they aren’t in use.) “You want the flexibility in how the space operates day to day, because out of 365 days, you’re maybe hosting a guest three nights,” Guerin says.

This “big comfy couch” from Article is our best-in-class sleeper sofa. It’s a pull-out style with a memory-foam mattress, which writers Erin Schwartz and Jeremy Rellosa (who both tested it in the Strategist office) say is supportive, has a pleasant firmness, and is thick enough that they couldn’t feel the metal bars through it. Schwartz also says it’s quite comfortable to sit on when it’s in couch mode. Most important of all, Schwartz appreciates that it does not look like a sleeper sofa.

If you have a bigger budget, Schwartz says American Leather is the brand that most furniture sellers will point you toward. (Not all its sofas are leather, though it does have an excellent leather selection.) What really makes its sleeper sofas stand out is the company’s patented conversion mechanism, which makes it especially easy to pull out the mattress (Schwartz says they did it with one hand!) and removes the potential of feeling metal bars under your back when sleeping.

Alternatively, “If you can fit a little daybed in your room or the kids’ room or something, then that’s an extra bed,” says blogger and small-space consultant Alison Mazurek. Set it up against the wall with a bunch of cushions to use it like a couch on a day-to-day basis, then lay it out flat as a bed when guests come over. She recommends Softline for daybeds, which are made with memory foam for comfort while sitting or sleeping.

Bautier makes a daybed that’s similar, albeit more expensive, than the Softline model above. Strategist contributor Fanny Singer ended up buying it after an extensive, months-long hunt for a non-ugly sleeper sofa.

[Editor’s note: This price is converted to USD from euros as of the latest update.]

Dressing a temporary guest bed with excellent bedding is an easy enhancement. If you have the space to store them, Lynch recommends having a dedicated set of guest sheets, because a matching set that complements your home décor will feel more intentional than pulling out random pieces of extra bedding and will show your guests that you thought of them ahead of time, Lynch says. For the top layer, Guerin suggests a few light blankets or quilts instead of a big fluffy comforter or duvet. Not only are thinner pieces easier for you to store and clean, but guests can add or remove layers as needed to maintain a comfortable sleep temperature. To top it all off, don’t forget to give your guests a quality pillow, which can make or break the comfort of a bed.

At just $50 for a queen-size set, these 100 percent cotton sateen sheets from Target’s Threshold line come highly recommended by Strategist writer Lauren Ro, who says they don’t feel cheap at all despite their low price — when she first tested them, she was surprised by how substantial they felt.

This two-pack of Beckham Hotel pillows is a longtime Strategist best seller, and deservedly so. The pillows have a fluffy, hotel-pillow feel but, crucially, provide actual neck support. They can work for multiple sleeping positions — back-, side-, and stomach-sleeping Strategist staffers have all tested and liked them — and are often on sale. Plus, they are fully machine washable, so you can pop them in the laundry between guests’ visits without any worry.

This quilt from Parachute is one of our favorites because it’s nice-looking and the perfect weight — warm but not overly bulky. One side is linen, the other cotton percale.

This soft knit cotton throw is as versatile as it is sophisticated. Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens enjoys using it both indoors, where it has a permanent spot next to her couch, and outdoors, when it’s just barely warm enough to lounge in the yard.

To keep dedicated guest pillows and bedding in storage, Lynch suggests vacuum-seal bags. Put all the bedding together in one bag, seal it, and stick it in your closet. Everything will be ready and in one spot the next time you host.

If you don’t have space for extra bedding, it’s all about repurposing what you already have. Mazurek uses a complementary mix of white and neutral sheets in her house, so when she make a bed for a guest, their bedding looks cohesive. She also recommends finding creative ways to keep “extra” items around; for example, Mazurek has two pillows on each of her kids’ beds so that she can occasionally pull one off for a guest to use without having to “store” them. If you don’t have an inch of space to spare, Mazurek advises phoning a friend — someone you know probably has an extra that you could borrow for a few nights.

After a literal place to sleep, making a space inviting and cozy can be as simple as making your guests feel “considered.”

It’s easy to forget that even people who travel light still show up with stuff — and they’ll need a place to keep that stuff during their stay. Even a single, emptied-out dresser drawer or a bit of closet space can help. Lynch also advises taking a nod from hotels and investing in a luggage rack: They fold up for easy storage when not in use and give guests a place other than the floor where they can open their bag or suitcase.

Guerin advises leaving a stack of fresh towels where your guests can easily find them, either on their bed or with any extra bedding you’ve got laid out for them. Whatever you do, don’t wait until they are ready to shower to start rummaging around for clean washcloths and bath sheets.

As with bedding, it’s nice to have a dedicated set of guest bath towels if you can swing it. Frontgate’s towels are our favorite affordable towels; Ro owns them in white and reports that still look nice after three years of “near constant” use.

I also recommend adding some basic hand towels and washcloths.

If you have the luxury of time and forethought, you should invest in versatile furniture like a multifunctional set of nesting tables or stools that can double as nightstands when needed. If you don’t, you’ll need to get creative with what you already have, say, by clearing off a coffee table or an end table and placing it next to the bed you’ve set up.

Lynch is a big advocate of using nesting tables to instantly add extra surface space where guests can set things down without feeling like they are disrupting your home. The largest table in a set may even work as a luggage rack, while the smallest becomes a bedside table.

Lynch also recommends storage ottomans as a way to give guests a spot for some of their stuff (or as a place to keep the guest bedding) and serve as an extra seat too.

Speaking of extra seats, Mazurek typically uses a couple Field Stools from Sundays as side tables but clears them off to use as stools when company comes. They could just as easily become nightstands when it’s time for bed.

Even if you are especially short on floor space, a big, sturdy tray on a couch or chair near to your guests’ bed can be a workable “nightstand” — and will be much more preferable than putting their stuff on the floor or trying to find a stable spot for their phone or a glass of water.

Guests don’t want to feel like an inconvenience to their host, so think ahead about what they might need and do your best to make it readily available. Make sure your outlets are visible and accessible, because no one wants to be moving furniture just to charge their phone. If your outlets aren’t obvious or easy to get to, plug in an extra-long charger or extension cord before your guests arrive.

In addition to outlets, make sure guests have easy access to a lamp. “Even if they’ve been there a number of times, most people don’t know how to navigate your house in the dark,” Guerin says. Bonus points for one that’s portable so they can move it around as needed.

Mazurek uses this portable light for her overnight guests. “You can carry it around like a lantern, so if they need to get around in your house, it’s really nice,” she says. It has three settings, so they can toggle the brightness.

The Casper Glow Light is a similarly portable option. Guests can simply flip it over to turn it on or off or twist it to dim.

Even if it’s not portable, place an easy-to-turn-on lamp like this LED desk lamp near your guests’ bed so they can turn in without getting up and searching for a wall switch.

Don’t underestimate the usefulness of a clip-on book light, like the Strategist-favorite Hooga, if space is especially tight.

These expert-recommended finishing touches will make them feel as welcome and as comfortable as possible, no matter how small your home is.

Mazurek and Guerin both recommend setting out a carafe of water and glasses so your guests can get a drink at night without having to search your kitchen cabinets in the dark.

If possible, Guerin recommends emulating a high-end hotel by providing luxuries like a bathrobe or slippers for your guests to use, along with a basket of goodies they might have forgotten, like extra toiletries or a sleep mask. She often saves sample-size beauty products to give to her friends when they visit as a little travel pick-me-up.

A waffle robe, like this one from Quince, will be smaller to store than a big, fluffy one if you decide to buy a dedicated guest robe.

Parachute’s Turkish cotton slippers wouldn’t be out of place at a high-end hotel, but they’re under $50 and fully machine washable.

A silk eye mask will add a touch of fanciness, even if they are sleeping on an air mattress in the living room, while helping block light from windows that may not have sleep-friendly curtains or shades.

Providing a sound machine is almost guaranteed to help them sleep better in an unfamiliar space, especially if you live on a noisy street.

As a counter to throw blankets for extra warmth, have a small fan ready for guests who run warm. Strategist writer Tembe Denton-Hurst recommends this inexpensive Honeywell fan, which she’s been using since 2016. It’s small enough to place on a desk or nightstand.

Smaller homes tend to lack privacy — and often have only one bathroom —so Guerin advises adding a folding screen or room divider: “If you don’t want to come out of your bedroom and immediately look at your friend in a stage of undress, the screen is nice,” she says. Options range from pricey antique finds on eBay or Chairish to inexpensive versions from big-box retailers, so there’s lots of flexibility with price and style. If you don’t have a full-time need for the screen when you aren’t hosting, Guerin suggests folding it up and sliding it behind or under couch or bed or sticking it in the back of a closet.

When you’re hosting in a small space, it’s easy to focus on what you can’t provide to your guests. But the experts I spoke to all emphasized focusing on what you can give them.

“You want to make sure that you’re thinking about them beyond the night into the morning and making sure everybody feels like they can operate in the space without making a mess,” Guerin says. That could include picking up some fruit or pastries or bagels to set out for an easy breakfast if your guests wake up earlier than you. Or ensuring that coffee and tea are accessible (and showing your guests how to use your coffee-maker).

Mazurek, who lives in Vancouver, advises taking full advantage of where you live to show your guests a good time. If your home is on the smaller side, odds are you’re in a large, high-cost of living area — which comes with its own advantages. “We can run out in the morning and get the best pastry or the best coffee they’ve had in a long time,” Mazurek says. “It’s just reminding people that maybe we don’t have a perfect room for you, but we have these other great things to offer and that we are showing them what we love about the city.”

Above all, Lynch adds, don’t put too much pressure on yourself, and remember that most guests won’t be expecting a high-end hotel experience in your living room. “People aren’t coming to your home to see what you have. They’re coming to your home to see you,” she says.

entry.title: The 16 Very Best Rain Boots for Women
entry.summary: Because wet socks are the worst.
entry.content:
Unlike hiking or snow boots that have been treated with a durable water-repellent finish, rain boots are made from fully waterproof materials like plastic or vulcanized rubber. They tend to lack shoelaces, zippers, or any other points where water might leak in. “The less seams and stitches, the more a boot can be water-resistant,” explains Igor Burt, a footwear designer and lecturer at Otis College of Art and Design. The trade-off is that rain boots can be rather sweaty, and aren’t great for more athletic activities. What they do is keep your feet clean while you garden, fish, or trod around the park in inclement weather.

To find the best women’s rain boots, I asked a number of outdoorsy types which ones they recommend, then tested out those pairs for myself. Below, find the best options for every rainy day, from classic Wellingtons to cool Maine-mom-approved clogs. While you’re here, I’ve also written guides to the best raincoats and umbrellas.

Updated on November 11, 2026
These women’s rain boots have been updated with the latest availability and pricing. And I added Plasticana’s clogs to the list.

While the classic Wellington is close to knee-height, I found a range of boots with different height profiles that’ll still keep your feet dry when faced with shallower puddles. For gardening, experts I spoke with advised that short and mid-calf boots are easier to slip on and off than taller ones. I also like this more discreet style of rain boot for conquering city slush.

Because a totally utilitarian rain boot won’t be for everyone, I looked for a range of wet-season shoes that don’t sacrifice style for function. Some of those include a caramel-toned boot made from hemp plastic, colorful boots that’ll match your raincoat, and a couple of sleek and subtle styles that resemble ordinary Chelsea boots — except with extra water protection.

While it’s always a good idea to wear socks with rain boots in order to avoid blisters, I favored lined boots that offer a little added comfort. I looked for boots with add traction and grip as well as those that offer a little arch support and taper somewhat to the foot’s natural shape.

Profile: Tall | Design details: Iconic buckle and silhouette | Comfort: Fitted shape, polyester lining, lightweight

I always feel like a celebrity when slipping on Hunter’s tall, Glastonbury-ready boots and can understand why professional gardeners and British socialites alike swear by them. Available in a spectrum of bright colors that will cheer you up on overcast days, the heritage brand’s rain boots are made to last and wipe down easily to retain their good looks. “No worries if they get muddy or dirty — a quick spray with a hose cleans them up in a snap,” says Southern California organic gardener and YouTuber CaliKim. Blogger Heidi Grey adds that they have a solid rubber construction, “so you don’t get any leakage at all.” These boots, while practical, are also very sleek. Karrie Meiklereid, creative director of The Style Room, calls Hunter “the go-to brand for rain boots.” CaliKim says, “Pulling them on always puts a smile on my face.” I find them to be surprisingly lightweight and flexible yet very waterproof due to their seamless rubber construction. The soles are bouncy and grippy with a slight heel, and the profile sits very high — you could plunge literally knee-deep in mud while wearing these and come away from it with a clean pair of jeans. They fit true to size.

Profile: Mid-calf | Design details: Iconic buckle and silhouette | Comfort: Fitted shape, polyester lining, lightweight

As much as I like the tall Hunter boots above, I don’t live on a farm, and it can be an imposition to pull them on every time I leave my apartment. Luckily, the brand also makes shorter boots with the same seamless rubber construction. I’ve been testing these out, too, and while they don’t provide knee-high splash protection, they’re very comfortable and completely waterproof. They have the same narrow fitted shape and grippy lugged soles as the original boots, and yes, they also come in lots of pretty colors that’ll stand out on gray days.

Profile: Tall | Design details: Classic silhouette, burnt-caramel color | Comfort: Tapered and supportive fit

Plasticana’s Wellies (constructed from recycled vinyl and hemp) are almost as status-y as Hunter’s but a little more affordable. They’re also slightly shorter and wider in fit, which makes for a more casual look. Strategist contributor Chantel Tattoli has “trotted all over rainy Paris, in the muddy countryside, and along Norman seashores” in hers, maintaining their sheen every now and then with a little linseed oil. They even earned a spot in her suitcase on a trip to Norway. She says the boots are comfortably fitted to the ankle, lightweight yet waterproof, and truly beautiful to look at. The hemp plastic they’re made from is “caramel-toned, like the fired sugar on crème brûlée — which tracks, because Plasticana’s color comes from the cooking of the sugar in the hemp fiber.”

Profile: Tall | Design details: Slightly curved silhouette, block heel | Comfort: Adjustable buckle fit, leather lining, full-length zip

Hunter boots may be worn by celebrities at muddy music festivals, but French boot-making brand Le Chameau’s Wellingtons are the rainy-day footwear of choice around the Cotswalds and in the gardens of Balmoral castle. Each pair is crafted by hand from thick natural rubber with a leather lining and thick bouncy sole; after hearing them praised by various posh people, I tried a pair on for myself, and I have to admit they’re as comfortable and supportive as the high price tag suggests they should be. Even better, they’re easy to slip on, thanks to a water-sealed zip that runs down the length of the boot. An adjustable buckle also tightens the boots around your calves for added waterproofing in deep puddles. Would I recommend them for everybody? Absolutely not, as every other pair of boots on this list is just as waterproof. But if you can spare the expense and happen to be living in a very rainy climate, they might just be worth it for the daily sense of luxury. Not a bad gift idea, either.

Profile: Tall | Design details: A happy frog | Comfort: Wide calf profile, woven PVC lining, Italian suede insole

Priced more affordably than the Le Chameaus above, Wellipets still have a British royal heritage: Princess Diana as well as young Princes Harry and William were spotted wearing them in the 1980s. More recently, my fellow Strategist writer Dominique Pariso became the happy owner of a pair, and she says that they’re both practical and delightful. “Aside from the joy these bring me and everyone else who sees them,” she says, “they’re great for wide calves.” While the slim-fitting profile of Hunter boots means that they have to be shimmied on and off, you can slide your feet right in and out of these in seconds. Then continue your rainy walk, ready for compliments from passersby.

Profile: Mid-calf | Design details: Roll-top | Comfort: Breathable lining, high-traction outsole

With a high-traction sole and comfortable lining, these boots are a reliable favorite of gardeners everywhere. “I’m a huge fan of Muck Boots,” says ecologist and botanist Becky Searle, adding that the Muckster II is “light, flexible and very comfortable,” with a mid-rise profile, excellent grip, breathable lining, and superior debris-shedding capability in the garden and beyond. These rain boots even have a roll-down top that turns them into an ankle-height waterproof shoe. Searle wears hers while in the garden, walking her dog, or picking up her kids from school. But if you just can’t stand the feel of rubber boots around your feet while you’re pulling weeds, gardeners we’ve spoken to also recommend Blundstones as a comfier and similarly mudproof alternative.

Profile: Tall | Design details: | Two-tone look | Comfort: Cushioned midsole, odor-repelling treatment, fleece lining, extra grip

While a waterproof boot makes sense for trudging through snow, most of the pairs listed here aren’t warm or grippy enough to be worn on freezing-cold days. These Bogs, as tested by Montana-based Strategist contributing writer Maggie Slepian, are the exception. As she writes, they look like an average pair of rain boots but are lined with warm fleece and armed with grippy lugs on the bottom for treading on ice. And as a bonus, they’re actually way easier to walk around in than normal snow boots because they “don’t rely on wide toe caps, reinforced liners, and felted insulation.”

Profile: Tall | Design details: Minimalist | Comfort: -10 degrees Fahrenheit temperature rating

When considering work-ready waterproof boots, I turned to Ben Shryock, chief ranger of the Alaska State Parks Kodiak region. He told me that these acid and chemical-resistant Xtratufs are his only choice and daily go-to: “They are the most comfortable and durable rubber boots I’ve found. You can find them for sale in almost any coastal Alaskan town.” He says that if you do happen to step in some water that goes over the 15-inch mark, they’ll air out fast — “much faster than leather boots.” Trying out a pair for myself, I found they have a slightly wider, more flexible fit than the Hunter boots above, though they’re the same height. This makes them somewhat easier to slip on and off. You can also roll them down to the calves if needed, exposing a cute print on the neoprene interior.

Profile: Short | Design details: Multiple colors | Comfort: Waterproof rubber, antimicrobial neoprene liner

Xtratuf’s lower-profile deck shoes are as waterproof as the pair above yet a little more practical for everyday life. Maine–based photographer Bea Helman (whose husband happens to be an oyster farmer) loves hers, saying that she wears them every single day (“rain or no rain”) and they’re perfect for both mud and snow. Beloved by deckhands, these ankle boots have slip-resistant soles that’ll come in handy whether you’re trawling for shellfish or not. I wore these through winter, sometimes alternating with Xtratuff’s fleece-lined versions on snow days. I love the neoprene gusset and pull tabs around the ankle, which makes them easy to put on and take off. They’re lightweight yet have a flat, solid sole. And to battle that sweaty rain-boot feeling, they have an antimicrobial liner that helps regulate foot temperature.

Profile: Short | Design details: Discreet Chelsea style | Comfort: Neoprene lining

These stealthy Chelsea boots from Merry People are actually fully waterproof. I tried them out for myself and found that their neoprene lining makes them much softer and cozier than other options. They have a slightly wider fit and higher profile than the Xtratuf deck shoes and are obviously much more city-friendly. They’re favorites of well-attired gardening types, like Amber Grossman, North Carolina gardener and creator of BlackGirlsGardening. “They’re just so comfortable and easy to clean,” she says of her pair. Katie Parks, who grows her own food on one acre in the Sierra Nevada Mountains in Northern California and is known in the gardening world as Freckles and Sprouts, likes the brand. Her Bobbi Rain Boots “hold up well to our heavy clay soil that clumps to your boots in wet weather, and they have a nice grip so I never slip.” She points out that ankle boots are easier to get off than knee-highs, plus, “they are cute enough to wear out as well,” she says. “I get compliments on them all the time!”

Profile: Short | Design details: Multiple colors | Comfort: Waterproof PVC

These sleek and surprisingly affordable Chelsea rain boots could easily be mistaken for their (less waterproof and pricier) leather counterparts. Made from lightweight PVC, with a pull tab and flexible elastic that makes them easy to put on and take off, these shoes are practical yet pretty enough to be worn out on rainy evenings. “They’re my best work-to-dinner boot,” says Helman. I like that they’re available in classic black as well as a number of more cheerful colors.

Profile: Very short | Design details: Slip on, pull tab | Comfort: Cushioned sole

Tall, rubbery rain boots can be annoying to pull on and off for quick trips to the store or when taking the dog out, which is why I decided to try this pair of not-quite-clogs from Bogs. These minimal boots provide enough ankle coverage to avoid minor splashes, and the cushioned platform footbed lends additional elevation. Yet unlike a knee-high pair of Hunters or even the slightly taller Chelseas above, these are super-easy to keep by the door and slip on and off while standing. If you do need to use your hands, the heavy-duty pull tabs and (highly waterproof) elastic gussets will help.

Profile: Short | Design details: Lacing, visible stitching | Comfort: Cozy lining

Grey says that these handmade boots, from Danish line Ilse Jacobsen, offer a fun contrast to the standard Hunter silhouette. She calls the minimal, lace-up style “super-Scandinavian.” Meiklereid agrees: “I love the lace-up as an alternative to the typical pull-on rain boot.” These boots have cozy faux-Sherpa lining, come in an adorable array of colors, and are made from sustainably sourced natural rubber (be sure to oil them from time to time). The visible stitching on their soles recalls Doc Martens.

Profile: Short | Design details: Preppy, classic silhouette | Comfort: High-traction, supportive shape

Made-in-Maine L.L.Bean duck boots are just as iconic as Hunter’s contribution to the rain boot canon, albeit polar opposite in their preppy vintage aesthetic. Originally designed for wet-weather hunting trips, these leather and rubber boots are highly durable and undeniably waterproof. Dana Landon of It’s My Darlin’ says she’s “been wearing these for rain, slush, and mud since high school. I never get sick of them and they last forever.”

Profile: Low | Design details: Multiple colors | Comfort: Waterproof leather and membrane layer, lugged sole

Helman is an L.L.Bean fan — it’s compulsory when living in Maine — but she prefers these discreet and highly durable slip-ons to the classic duck shoe. Called “storm chasers” for a reason, these clogs are “absolutely waterproof” despite their low profile, she says. And because they lack the bulk of boots, you can easily wear them all year long across different weather conditions. These highly utilitarian shoes are perfect for winter. They even have traction on their thick rubber soles that can hold its own against ice and snow.

Profile: Low | Design details: Three colorways, neutral everyday look | Comfort: Unlined, easy to slip on and off

Plasticana’s hemp plastic clogs are more practical for everyday wear than the brand’s taller rain boots above but just as nice looking. I love my pair so much that I recently took a four-day trip to the Catskills and brought them as my only shoes. I wore them apple picking in a muddy field, out to dinner at several fancy restaurants, and even to the sauna. They have a wide and flexible fit that makes them easy to slip on and off, surprisingly good sole traction (though they’re not as winter-ready as the L.L.Bean Storm Chasers), and a slight heel that adds a touch of elegance to even your least impressive gardening outfit. I’d suggest going half a size down.

entry.title: How Lumify Found Its Way Into Every Celebrity’s Makeup Routine
entry.summary: Alex Rodriguez, Jennifer Lopez, Sydney Sweeney, and Naomi Campbell all use the humble drugstore eye drops.
entry.content:
What would you say if we told you an eye drop is one of the most consistently recommended products? The one thing celebrities and beauty insiders almost always want to tell us about? That has been the case with Lumify. We started hearing about the $15 drugstore anti-redness eye drops when they launched in 2018, and the mentions haven’t stopped since. Our very first celebrity recommender, Catherine Zeta-Jones, put it this way in her “What I Can’t Live Without”: “I’m not sacrificing looks for comfort — though I would totally use them if they did sting because they seriously lighten and brighten my eyes.” In the years since, we’ve heard about Lumify drops from Courteney Cox, Alan Cumming, Ming-Na Wen, Alex Rodriguez, and dozens of beauty professionals, such as makeup artist Scott Barnes. Brooke Shields, Nick Jonas, Sydney Sweeney, and Jessica Alba are also fans. The recommendations were so consistent and nonstop that enough became enough: We needed to know how these eye drops ended up everywhere and became so indispensable.

Chances are you don’t think about red eyes too often unless you’re prone to getting them. But it’s a bigger deal for people who are photographed for a living. “When you are doing an Oscar campaign or a ton of press as an onscreen talent, there’s a very demanding schedule,” says makeup artist Vincent Oquendo, whose clients include Hailey Bieber, Kendall Jenner, and Gigi and Bella Hadid. That’ll definitely drive up the eye redness. “The way that’s perceived on-camera is that they’re unwell,” he says.

Before Lumify, makeup artists smuggled contraband whitening eye drops from Asia and Europe into the U.S. Well-known American versions like Visine left the eye feeling dryer in the longer term, while the imports felt more hydrating. However, they did come with other drawbacks. The menthol-laced Rohto from Japan stung like crazy. Collyre from France was tinted with methylene blue, a synthetic dye used to treat a rare blood disorder that is definitely not approved for use on eyeballs. Oquendo remembers trying mentholated eye drops and complaining to colleagues that they didn’t feel good. “‘Beauty is pain,’ other makeup artists told me, but I didn’t really feel like that should be the case,” he says.

The redness-reliever category existed for decades before Lumify, but many traditional products, again like Visine, caused rebound redness and reduced effectiveness over time. They’re not a product ophthalmologists recommend regularly, though they tolerate occasional use. “They don’t address the root cause of redness,” says Dr. Julie Chung, a California-based ophthalmologist. Her job is to figure out what causes redness — dry eyes, allergies, or inflammation — and treat it.

In December 2017, the Food and Drug Administration gave clearance to Bausch + Lomb, the eye-health-products company, to launch Lumify, a solution with the active ingredient brimonidine tartrate at a 0.025% concentration. Lumify is different from previous redness relievers in that it brightens the sclera, or the white of the eye, by constricting the small veins on the surface that contribute to redness, while maintaining necessary blood and oxygen flow.

“Traditional redness relievers constrict both arteries and veins on the surface of the eye,” says Mayssa Attar, senior vice-president, pharmaceuticals and consumer R&D at Bausch + Lomb, and that results in redness rebounding worse than before. That’s because the drops block oxygen-rich blood and nutrients from reaching the surface of the eye. When the effect wears off, the blood vessels dilate larger than before to restore normal blood flow.

Ophthalmologists have used brimonidine tartrate in higher doses to treat glaucoma for decades and have known about its serendipitous brightening side effect, but no one had thought to leverage that for cosmetic use. As a glaucoma specialist who’s very familiar with the ingredient, Chung didn’t see it coming that a drop she prescribed to prevent blindness would be used by people to look pretty. She laughed when a makeup artist asked to use it before a shoot. “My eyes aren’t particularly red,” she says, “but I was shocked at how ‘awake’ I looked and how cosmetically appealing it is.” She even ended up recommending it to the Strategist (with several caveats).

In the years before launch, the Lumify team found out makeup artists were, as Ferris puts it, “seeking out specialty products internationally.” They had heard about Lumify from beauty blogs, online forums, and product reviews, and this was one of the first clues they had that it could have broader appeal. “It gave us confidence that we were tapping into an existing behavior and need, rather than trying to create one,” says John Ferris, the president of North America’s consumer division at Bausch + Lomb.

Bausch + Lomb suspected they had a winner, mostly because Lumify worked quickly and was relatively safer than other redness relievers. Plus a theme had emerged from their consumer testing: People were interested in brighter eyes, and eye appearance mattered within beauty culture.

The only problem was that neither editors nor consumers thought of eye drops as a beauty product. There was nothing inherently aspirational or glamorous about standing too close to one’s bathroom mirror dribbling in eye drops, mouth agape. Beauty editors who at the time were the most reliable brand-to-consumer use translators, shared that view and weren’t keen on writing about eye care.

Lumify realized makeup artists would be the right professionals to partner with. They operate in an environment where every detail matters, and their eyedrop-smuggling operation proved they had identified a need for the product and were going out of their way to obtain it. They held influence over editors and celebrities and, via that trickle-down effect, could influence public perception. “They had the credibility to help reframe how the category could be perceived,” says Ferris.

In 2017, Oquendo was one of the industry’s most in-demand makeup artists; he’d worked with Paris Jackson for the Met Gala, Lily Collins for the Cannes red carpet, and Ashley Graham on America’s Next Top Model. He was respected by his peers and wasn’t a gatekeeper — he freely shared product recommendations with editors and fellow artists.

He was also “an eye guy.” Oquendo’s skill was creating makeup that elongated the eyes while simultaneously making them look wide open, as he’s done for Hailey Bieber. Oquendo also knew how to leverage social media well and pulled back the curtain to give his audience peeks into how the celebrity sausage was made. “He had the credibility to evaluate the product and introduce it to audiences that influence beauty trends and product discovery,” says Ferris. Lumify had found its first ambassador.

In May 2018, Oquendo was on the film-festival circuit in Cannes and Toronto doing celebrity makeup. The brand sent him off loaded with product: “I had a giant Ziploc full of Lumify, and my international actresses were thrilled because they couldn’t get it overseas.” Many demanded multiples.

When on-set crews see celebrities ask for something, they’re immediately curious, so Lumify landed in the hands of hairdressers, stylists, and anyone who asked for it on any set Oquendo was on. He remembers distributing over 60 vials of Lumify to makeup artists and celebrities in the course of a week. He was handing them out like candy.

Lumify was also seeding product to more than a hundred leading makeup artists, and Ferris credits that as the one thing that really moved the needle on mass attention. Recommendations started appearing in the press from artists like Sandy Linter and Gita Bass. Later, Donni Davy, Patrick Starrr, Ash K. Holm, Daniel Martin, and Hung Vanngo all went on record about using it in their pro kits.

Even formerly reluctant beauty editors came onboard quickly: Allure was one of the outlets to review it positively the year it launched. The brand also turned to influencers and creators like Elsa Hosk, Winnie Harlow, Olivia Culpo, Kaley Cuoco, and Stephanie Ledda for early momentum. Alix Earle has mentioned it several times over the years, and it has been on Gracie Abrams’s, Jake Shane’s, and Katie Feeney’s feeds. Lumify began appearing in places the brand hadn’t reached out to, including in the background on shows like Keeping Up With the Kardashians and America’s Sweethearts: Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders.

The brand has since launched Lumify Eye Illuminations, a line of three products including a micellar water, an eye cream, and a lash and brow serum, trying to extend its success into the skin-care world, but the eye drops remain the hero product by far.

Oquendo remembers randomly scrolling Instagram back in 2022 and landing on Jennifer Lopez sharing her beauty routine with Vogue. She held up her bottle of Lumify and popped a drop into each eye. Oquendo hasn’t worked with Lopez but knows people who do, and he knew it was genuine testimony: “It was such a proud moment that I was a part of this process of [getting it to her] because the only way she was gonna get it was through her makeup artist putting it on her.”

entry.title: The Best Automatic Feeders for Cats, According to Cat People
entry.summary: Including simple and higher-tech options for both wet and dry food.
entry.content:
There are plenty of ways to feed your cat, depending on both the cat’s needs and your schedule. The simplest approaches, like free feeding or serving each meal in a bowl, often work well. But if they aren’t feasible due to your busy or unpredictable schedule, a need to control your cat’s meals for health reasons, or simply because you don’t want to be bothered by meowing before your alarm goes off every morning, an automatic cat feeder can be a major help. According to certified advanced feline-behavior specialist Michelle Danahy, most cats love the routine of feeding, whether that’s you cracking open a can or an automatic feeder going off — so if a feeder helps you to maintain your cat’s routine, then it can be a beneficial tool.

That being said, automatic feeders aren’t necessarily right for every household. They are generally more expensive than a simple bowl, require more complex cleaning, and can remove an opportunity for bonding with your cat, says Jennifer Van de Kieft, a cat behaviorist and nutritionist. And while they can be extremely handy, cat-behavior consultant Dr. Mikel Delgado cautions that since technology can fail, you shouldn’t think of an automatic feeder as a replacement for a cat-sitter when you’re away from home for extended periods of time.

To find the best automatic cat feeders, I asked Danahy, Van de Kieft, Delgado, and other cat experts and owners about their tips on how to choose the right automatic cat feeder and which ones they like best.

Deciding whether to use an automatic feeder and choosing the right automatic feeder ultimately comes down to figuring out what works for you and your cat(s), so there is no single “best” option for everyone. What your cat eats, how much and how often you feed them, how many cats you have, and the specific features you’re looking are all important factors, says Delgado.

The two main types of feeders are programmable and gravity feeders. If you are using an automatic version to monitor your cat’s diet for weight management or another health concern, the experts generally favor a programmable feeder, as you can more strictly portion how much food your cat eats and when. Gravity feeders continually replenish the bowl as your cat eats, which makes it difficult to know how much they are consuming, says certified cat-behavior consultant Kristiina Wilson.

Another type of feeder you might consider is an RFID- or microchip-activated feeder, which only allows the “registered” cat to eat from the feeder by scanning a collar tag or the pet’s microchip. Additionally, some feeders have high-tech features like app-based controls, video, or audio. It’s also important to consider the nitty-gritty, practical elements of a feeder, like how easy it is to clean, whether the feeder has a backup power source, and whether it is secure enough that a motivated cat (or other pets in your home) can’t break into the food reserve.

PetLibro’s Granary feeder has just about every feature you could ask for. Danahy uses it with her own cats and told me many of her clients use it too. (We also recommend it in our guide to the best automatic feeders for dogs.) It has a five-liter capacity and works with most dry food — PetLibro’s maximum recommended kibble size is 15 x 15 millimeters. With the PetLibro app, you can schedule up to ten separate meals per day; for each meal, you can customize exactly how much food is dispensed. Being able to schedule specific portions can be very beneficial for cats that are on a specific diet. Danahy says that since creating a schedule for her feeder in the app, she rarely looks at it, so it doesn’t require constant monitoring. But if you’d like some reassurance that your cat is eating its meals as expected when you’re away, there is a built-in camera that can help ease that anxiety; the Granary also has a motion detector that can send you alerts when your cat walks nearby. An audio feature allows you to “call” your cat, but most of the experts I spoke to warned me that using it is more likely to scare cats than comfort them. The app will also send you alerts when the food supply is low or if there is a malfunction or a power outage.

The Granary is primarily powered by plugging it into an outlet, but it has a battery backup option, which is a feature Van de Kieft recommends looking for in any automatic feeder that you’ll be relying on while away from home. And while most of the device is made of plastic, it’s nice that the food bowl is made from stainless steel, which tends to be more hygienic than plastic and less likely to cause cats to develop chin acne. (PetLibro also makes a two-bowl version of the Granary, though Van de Kieft cautions that cats generally do not like to eat closely to one another, so dual feeders can cause unnecessary stress between cats.) Overall, the Granary is a splurgy option that likely offers more features than the average cat owner requires, but for those who need to specifically portion their cat’s meals, who want the ease of app-based controls, or who appreciate having a built-in camera to check in while away from home, it’s a solid choice.

If you want an automatic feeder with the majority of important features the experts recommend without spending more than you need to, the Oneisall is a great less-expensive option. Kerrie McKeon, lead feline-care specialist at Bideawee, used it during a cat-sitting gig and says it works well, is easy to operate, and was loved by the cats. It’s a little smaller than the Granary, with a 3.5-liter capacity. But it shares many of the same features, like a stainless-steel bowl, app-based controls that allow scheduling up to ten meals per day, and a battery backup. The single-bowl version of the Oneisall does not have a camera or any motion-detecting capabilities like the Granary does. There is a two-bowl version, which has a camera and audio, but again, dual feeders aren’t a good fit for most cats.

For multi-pet households, a microchip-activated feeder can ensure each pet eats its food and its food only. Danahy says this can be especially helpful for cats on a specific diet, cats that need medication with their food, or cats that eat each other’s food. The SureFeed is a microchip-activated feeder that comes recommended by Wilson, Delgado, and senior editor Michael Berk. “In a multi-cat household like mine, food competition and resource access can be significant sources of tension,” says Wilson. “A microchip feeder can help reduce that competition by giving each cat reliable access to their own food.” Delgado says it keeps her “hungrier” cat from eating all of her sisters’ food and allows her to track her cats’ eating habits in the corresponding app. The lid of the sealed food bowl lifts only when the pet whose microchip is connected to the SureFeed approaches it. (You can also use an RFID collar tag from PetSure if your cat is not microchipped, but Delgado says she prefers the microchip method, as a tag can fall off a collar.)

Berk says he likes that the SureFeed has a lot of flexibility for training cats to use it, as the moving parts can be off-putting at first. The feeder has a “Training Function” that allows cats to get accustomed to eating from it by slowly incorporating the lid opening and closing until they come to expect the lid to open when they approach the feeder.

Unlike the other automatic feeders on this list, the SureFeed doesn’t hold a reserve of food, so you have to manually add each serving to the dishes. In the app, you can set portion limits by weight and the feeder will let you know when you’ve added the correct amount of food, which is helpful for cats that need to eat strict portion sizes. The SureFeed works with both wet and dry food, since it has to be refilled for every meal. Berk notes that you can swap out the bowl if you want — SureFeed sells stainless-steel and slow-feeder versions of the bowls that slot into the feeder. He also recommends adding the back shield if you have a very persistent food thief trying to edge in from the wrong side.

Most automatic feeders are designed for dry food, so if you want to provide your cat with timed portions of wet food, you’ll need a feeder specifically designed for that. Senior writer Michael Zhao likes this wet-food feeder from Closer Pets, which he started using after his cats learned to break into the simple mechanical timer feeder he previously tried. “One of our cats in particular will eat until he throws up if we leave out too much food,” Zhao says, “so we have to make the feedings small and space them out.” This feeder allows him to preportion meals and set the time when they are served. The controls are on the feeder, rather than in an app, and it runs on batteries. It can hold up to five servings — each compartment in the bowl has an 11.6-ounce capacity — and the bowl is dishwasher safe. The feeder also comes with ice packs to keep the food cold if needed. Van de Kieft says some cats won’t eat their food if it’s too cold, so she advises testing how your cat reacts to chilled wet food before using this type of feeder. And depending on the intervals of the meals, Zhao says the ice packs aren’t always necessary. Conveniently, while this feeder is geared toward wet food, it can also be used with dry food if you serve your cat both types.

If you’re looking for a simple, inexpensive feeder, Delgado recommends this one from PetSafe. She doesn’t give her cats all their meals in it, but she likes using it to schedule a snack in the morning to keep them from waking her up early begging for food. The feeder runs on batteries and has a simple mechanical timer that you can set up to 24 hours ahead. The lid simply pops open to give cats access to their meal. The bowl has two compartments, which each hold 1.5 cups of food. It is also dishwasher safe.

entry.title: My New Favorite 3-D Printer Is Ideal for Beginners and Experts Alike
entry.summary: The Bambu Labs P2S makes it easy for anyone to make almost anything — in multiple colors at once.
entry.content:
I’ve been experimenting with and using 3-D printers for over a decade now, but it always felt like work. It wasn’t until I bought and started using the Bambu Lab P2S that I actually started having fun with the hobby.

Prior to that, I’d owned Prusa and Creality printers that felt like more work than it was worth — it took so much time and effort to get good results that I wanted to quit. In fact, I flat out gave up on my Creality Ender 3 Pro and donated it to my local Goodwill.

The Bambu P2S’s ease of setup and use along with its reliable performance and print quality — something I can vouch for after putting several hundred hours of print time on it — combined with its affordable price are why it’s currently our top pick as the best 3-D printer overall.

You can get the P2S on its own, or for a couple of hundred bucks more you can pick up the the $649 Combo kit, which includes the AMS 2 Pro multi-material system. The AMS 2 Pro lets you load four spools of filament in different colors or materials and switch automatically between them, opening up the world of multicolored printing to everybody.

The P2S Combo arrives in a single box with the included AMS 2 Pro tucked securely inside the printer. Unboxing, setting it up, and running through the initial calibration process takes about an hour from start to finish.
Inside the box is a toolkit along with a getting-started guide that walks you through the process; if you prefer, you can also follow along online using Bambu’s P2S unboxing guide, complete with videos of each step.

You don’t need to be very technical to set it up. You’ll need to remove a few screws with the included tools, cut some zip ties, remove some foam inserts, connect some tubing and wires between the printer and AMS 2 Pro, and install the optional external spool holder.

After powering on the P2S for the first time, the five-inch display walks you through connecting the printer to your Wi-Fi, then binding it to your Bambu Lab account. Finally, you’re prompted to go through the initial calibration process, which takes about 40 minutes to complete.

Once that’s done, you can start printing right away. There are models already loaded in the printer’s storage that you can select from. It’s tradition that your first print on a new printer is the Benchy model, so that’s exactly what I did, selecting it from the printer’s file menu. Thirty minutes later, I had a successful print.

The P2S measures 15.4-by-16-by-18.8 inches and weighs just under 33 pounds. You’ll want to place it somewhere that’s stable, and preferably you won’t want to have to move it around a lot (if you do, make sure to go through the calibration process each time you move it).

The P2S is a CoreXY printer, meaning that the build plate (which holds the model you’re printing) moves up and down for each new layer on the Z-axis, while the toolhead (which dispenses the material) moves around the print bed on the X- and Y-axes.

That’s in contrast to the bed slinger design used in printers such as Bambu Lab’s A-series, which moves the build plate back and forth on the Y-axis, while the toolhead moves left to right and up and down on the X- and Z-axes, respectively.

While bed slingers tend to be cheaper, a CoreXY printer is more accurate and faster and often has an enclosed housing that prevents temperature swings that affect print quality.

The P2S has a single toolhead and comes fitted with a 0.4-mm “hotend,” or nozzle. That’s the nozzle size I use for nearly all of my prints (and most users stick with the stock nozzle). However, you can swap out the nozzle in under 30 seconds without any tools. You can go smaller with a 0.2-mm nozzle for finer prints, such as earrings or small figurines, or go bigger with a 0.6-mm nozzle for larger models and tools.The build plate in the P2S measures 256-by-256 mm, which has been big enough to print anything I want.

There’s a 1080p camera in the front-left corner of the housing that’s used to monitor for failed prints, livestream a print, or record a time-lapse video of a print to the printers internal storage. You can use a thumb drive to expand the printer’s 8GB of built-in storage, which is quickly taken up by print files and videos.

As for materials you can use with the P2S, well, the list is long. Staple filaments like PLA and PETG are supported, as are softer materials like TPU (ever seen the airless basketball? That’s printed with TPU), or more rugged materials such as ABS that’s often used when printing stuff you need to be sturdy, like shelves or tools.

The lone feature that would be a nice to have on the P2S is a heated chamber, which can aid in printing some materials, such as ABS. That’s a feature reserved for Bambu’s higher-end (and more expensive) printers, like the X2D. I’ve only missed having it a handful of times, and it isn’t at all necessary if you’re printing with PLA and PETG (which is more likely what you’ll be using). The enclosed print chamber alone is more than enough.

My favorite feature of the P2S — and it’s not even close — is its ability to print in multiple colors. I’ll never forget the first time I used the P2S for a multicolored print and how amazed I was. Not only did the final print look fantastic, but I just couldn’t get over how easy it was. I’d previously tried multiple color prints on a Prusa Mini+, but it was entirely manual and required babysitting the print to swap colors at different layers.

As mentioned above, the P2S Combo includes the AMS 2 Pro, the attachment that allows you to use multiple colors in the same print. The AMS 2 Pro enclosure sits on top of the printer, where it connects via a short cable and single PTFE tube. There are four slots inside, each one for a different spool of filament. That means you can put up to four different colors in the AMS and it’ll handle the filament changes during a print, swapping out one color for another each time it’s needed.

You can connect up to 4 AMS 2 Pros to the P2S, giving you the ability to print with up to 16 colors at a time — insane!

The downside to the P2S having a single nozzle is the amount of waste created with every multicolored print. Each time the printer needs to change filaments, it has to clear the nozzle of the previous color by extruding excess filament of the new color to ensure it’s clear. The end result is a pile of wasted filament, or, as it’s commonly referred to in the 3-D-printing community, “poop.” Clearing the nozzle also adds to the overall print time because each filament swap takes several minutes.

Higher-end printers with multiple print tools, such as Bambu Lab’s X2D, H2-series, or the just-released H3C, speed up the print time and create less waste, but they’re pricey. The H3C starts at $2,500, for instance.

3-D printing can be an intimidating hobby for newcomers. There’s a bunch of jargon that can make you feel like you need to learn a completely different language, and that doesn’t even take into account finding stuff you want to print.

Bambu Lab has done a lot to remove that friction via its software. For example, the Bambu Handy mobile app isn’t used to just monitor prints — you can browse the entire MakerWorld catalogue of models and projects, then send anything you like straight to the printer, all without ever having to worry about print settings. Better yet, you can do it from anywhere you have an internet connection.

While sitting at my desk writing this review, I browsed holiday-themed models, found one I liked, and started the print — all with three taps without ever leaving my desk and never having to worry about any settings at all. (Granted, I already had the proper colors loaded in the AMS 2 Pro, so that saved me a step.)

Find a model, press print: It could not get easier.

Of course, if you want to go deeper down the 3-D printing rabbit hole, you certainly can use the Bambu Studio app on your computer. Within Studio you can fine-tune print settings such as layer height, infill amount and type, and access other more technical settings.

But the secret sauce is the simple fact that you don’t ever have to do that — you’d be perfectly fine never opening Studio and doing everything from your phone.

The P2S has powered through hundreds of hours of my personal printing, and I’ve had virtually no issues (at least that weren’t self-caused). It’s been a huge change from my prior experiences with 3-D printers, and I’d recommend the P2S as a great option for beginners who want a printer to grow into while also checking all the boxes for anyone who’s been 3-D printing for a while and would appreciate an upgrade from an older, more finicky machine.

entry.title: How the Strategist Staff Caffeinates
entry.summary: Including espresso machines at multiple price points and an unleakable plastic-free cup for sipping on the go.
entry.content:
From drip coffee and pour-overs to espresso and energy drinks, there are many ways to get your caffeine fix. It takes a decent amount of research and practice to perfect a good cuppa or matcha at home, and I thought, who better to survey than my fellow colleagues here at the Strategist. So, for this installment of “Stuff We Buy Ourselves,” I asked staffers how they caffeinate throughout the day, whether that’s a flat white or oolong tea. Along with the drinks of their choice, I also wanted to hear about their setups: grinders, kettles, mugs, and all. Their recommendations are below, including espresso machines at multiple price points and an unleakable plastic-free cup for sipping on the go.

Have you really processed what an espresso drink costs at a third-wave café these days? Between the drink itself, sales tax, plus tip (not to mention a possible upcharge for non-cow’s milk), you’re lucky to walk out the door paying less than $7 for a flat white. Though $2,000 for the Breville Oracle Jet seems like a lot to spend on an espresso machine, I did the math, and assuming my wife and I each drink one to two drinks every day, it paid for itself in its first four months of use — and it’s still under warranty for another 20. Compared to other all-in-ones I’ve tried, this machine makes it easier to make more consistently great coffee drinks because it has an adjustable water temperature and a built-in distributor tool that ensures perfect prep every time. The dual ThermoJet water-heating system preheats in seconds instead of minutes — compared to a typical boiler-based system — and the responsive touchscreen makes it so easy to operate that I can use it one-handed while carrying my infant in the other arm.

As for beans, I’ve been trying a few different options using Trade Coffee’s discovery trial. I found the first roast from Boston’s Broadsheet to be a bit too dark for my taste, but I look forward to trying the lighter Blue Orchid Blend from Denver’s Huckleberry Roasters. When I’m feeling less adventurous, my standbys are the Time and Temperature blend from Tandem in Portland, Maine, and Pastime Coffee’s Sure Thing blend from Portland, Oregon. Both are available in convenient two-pound bags, which help save some money without being so large that they start to go stale before getting to the end.

The first thing I do when I get up in the morning is get the electric kettle going. I’ve had this Breville kettle since 2010; it doesn’t do anything fancy — you just press the one switch, and that starts the water heating, and it pings and switches off once the water is at a vigorous boil. I’ll usually turn it off myself when I hear the water just starting to boil, with the hopes that it’s somewhat short of 212 degrees (for better tea brewing).

I read earlier this year about the benefits of naturally occurring gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in certain types of oolong, the type of tea I already preferred as my source of caffeine, and have been drinking it weekday mornings ever since (it’s been about five months and counting). I find that, for me, it helps me stay focused and keeps the brain fog at bay. (The only reason I don’t drink it on the weekends is because I still like to drink other kinds of oolong and have a substantial stash I’m trying to work through.) Other kinds of oolong I find too caffeinated to drink more of or even to steep a second time later in the day, but the GABA oolong I’ll drink a second steeping of at midday or late in the afternoon, and I find it has no effect on my sleep (quite possibly, according to the research, it even helps).

I’ve been using this Finum tea strainer since 2015, and I’ve tried to switch to other strainers (woven brass ones, all stainless steel) that don’t have any plastic parts in them, but this one just works better than anything else.

My husband broke two of my favorite mugs this year, most recently this Heath Ceramics one, which at least is replaceable (the other was not). The proportions of it are just right in my hands, and it holds the perfect amount of tea for my purposes. I also like that the rim is not too thick.

I handle a lot of the Strategist’s coffee coverage, which means my kitchen consistently has a rotating cast of coffee makers, coffee grinders, and milk frothers — and I have opinions on all. But in my own daily life — when I’m not testing particular products — I rarely use the latter two. Maybe I shouldn’t be admitting this, but I buy pre-ground Dunkin’ beans most of the time because I think they make the most delicious coffee in the world when it comes to classic drip machines, which is my preference. (I do keep a Baratza grinder around for the moments where I find myself with a fancier bag of whole beans, and it works great.) As for the machines themselves, I had this OXO model (our Best in Class pick) on my counter for quite a while, but I recently swapped it out for Caraway’s new plastic-free model in order to write a review of it. And there are a few other models in boxes in my hallway waiting for their moment.

I’m a coffee lover, but never a coffee snob. For the past three years, I’ve started the day with either a flat white or long black made with my Breville Bambino Plus. It’s a nearly automatic home espresso machine that requires very little maintenance or know-how. I love it. A few people I’ve made coffee for over the years have been convinced to buy one after seeing it in action. Freshly ground beans are essential, and I use a discontinued Fellow grinder that the brand sent me ages ago. It’s okay, but I wish I had a Baratza. I like trying different beans each week from a Trade or Atlas subscription. I always sip from the same favorite Robert Gordon ceramic mug that my best friend sent me from Australia. I also like to drink tea while I write — the Diaspora Co. masala chai that comes in a set with an East Fork Kulhad is a real favorite. When I travel, I’ll take an Aeropress or the titanium Snow Peak French Press with me, but I draw the line at a travel grinder.

I am a Celsius acolyte. I drink one first thing in the morning, every morning, and as of my last check, I’ve ordered 53 cases over the past two years. It’s a little insane and I’m not proud of my consumption; one commenter even referred to Celsius as “fizzy speed,” but it works.

I have a complicated relationship with caffeine — I gave up espresso in 2019 (too jittery) and drank chai for years. I’ve also gone through phases of cutting it out entirely because it was affecting my sleep, but now I take low-dose melatonin and enjoy a daily matcha, sometimes two. My current setup starts with a small scoop (I stopped measuring) that I sift in this canister from Astrid Tea (it has entirely removed clumpy bits from my matcha). Then I shake that into a Pyrex mixing pitcher with a dash of boiling water from a Fellow kettle. Next, I whisk it with this bamboo one from Sorate.

If I’m taking it cold, I pour oat milk straight into the pitcher and then transfer to a glass. If I want a warm one, I’ll pour milk into Terra Kaffe’s milk frother, hit the matcha setting, let it swirl a bit first, and then add the matcha after a few seconds. I trade off between matcha (right now I like Sorate, Rishi, and Pique) and hojicha (from Cap Beauty or Kettl). The hojicha apparently has less caffeine. If I’m taking it to go, I’ll pour it into Fellow’s truly unleakable ceramic-lined cup (which my colleagues Jen and Michael pointed me to). It even has a little splash guard, which is good for driving. The Maho cup is newer to me, and while it will never compete with stainless steel for heat retention, it’s a very pleasant drinking experience. It’s completely plastic-free, has a secure silicone lid, keeps things warm, and feels very nice to sip from — no metallic taste, which is the reason I ordered it.

Here’s my fairly minimal setup. (I just moved into a new apartment about a month and a half ago.) I’m not a coffee snob by any means, but I do love my espresso machine. It’s supremely easy to use; it can pull single and double shots and make cold brew. Plus the water reservoir detaches so I can fill it up at the sink. I don’t have a grinder at the moment, so it’s ground beans right now; I simply go off vibes at the store, though Peet’s Alameda Morning is a favorite. I’m currently on the hunt for a knock box, so I’ve been using a deli container at the moment; please no judgment at this time. And for all the accoutrements: I use one of the millions of bamboo trays from Ikea that I’ve amassed over the years. My mug was made by my dear former pottery teacher, Shannon.

My home coffee-making (and consumption) habits have definitely evolved over the years; when I was still living with roommates, I had an OXO French press I used religiously until one roommate mysteriously broke it. When my now-husband and I first moved in together, we used a Cuisinart, which did the job, but I didn’t know what we were missing until he got us a Moccamaster for Christmas one year. The coffee was smoother and brewed faster, and the machine overall looked nicer on the counter too. Freshly ground beans using this grinder each time helps a lot as well.

The one constant between my different coffee setups over the years has been a Trade coffee subscription. I truly love it so much. Back when I was grinderless, it was helpful to be able to select what brewing method I used and Trade would send ground beans that worked specifically for my French press. Now that we grind them ourselves, I like that I’m able to order a mix of different beans from roasters across the country. I’m no coffee snob, so I can rarely notice a difference in tasting notes, but it’s a nice surprise to see what you get each month.

My current setup is admittedly very gray, so if the Moccamaster ever dies (which, I hope not!), we’ll probably go for a more colorful one next time.

I start nearly every weekday with a cup of hot coffee with some oat milk. I just started testing De’Longhi’s All-in-One coffee and espresso machine, and it’s already made my mornings easier. (I was previously using a Moka pot, which I’m still keeping around for camping trips.) The coffee maker is as automatic as it gets, and the warmer keeps an entire pot surprisingly toasty for hours. If I have some extra time in the morning, I like the option of a latte instead. Again, the espresso side is very intuitive and includes an adjustable steam wand that doubles as a hot-water dispenser. This truly feels like the Swiss Army knife of coffee makers. I have yet to try the cold-brew or cold-foam settings, but I have high hopes based on how the other features have performed.

In the past, I’ve been grossly unpicky when it comes to beans, usually grabbing the cheapest bag from Trader Joe’s or Ralph’s. But I’ve been spoiled with good coffee that my boyfriend gets on subscription from Little Dreamer, a shop in Houston. The blends I’ve tried — Day Dreamer and Oaxaca — are rich and bold. I’m no coffee snob (I couldn’t tell you specific notes), but this has elevated my morning cup in a way that makes going back to grocery-bought varieties near impossible. Grinding coffee beans fresh has also been a game changer. The Cuisinart is easy to use and allows for different grind settings, depending on if I want regular coffee or espresso. My only qualm is that it’s on the louder side. I store a couple days’ worth of fresh grounds in two Pyrex canisters.

I usually need something to get me through my afternoon slump. I’ve found that a third or fourth coffee in the afternoon usually results in bad sleep. Now I switch to matcha later in the day and have recently started making it at home. This setup has everything I need to whisk up a high-quality matcha hot or iced. It gives me that extra bit of energy I need to get through the day without any jitters, and so far it hasn’t affected my ability to fall asleep.

I was recently gifted these ceramic mugs from the Los Angeles–based home-goods studio Earl. They are beautiful but hefty, so I don’t feel I have to be too precious with them. After stopping by Smorgasburg LA’s Filipino market recently, I also added a new mug from Ten of Cups Ceramics to my collection with the Filipino star on it. And on the rare occasion I take my coffee to go, I use this ceramic mug with a silicone lid and sleeve from Nova Ceramics.

I never thought of myself as a fully automatic espresso-machine person, but after trying out a similar model at my parents’ house for over a year and looking forward to using it whenever I visited them, I decided to request a sample. And I am not exaggerating when I say it has changed my life for the better.

My husband likes to make a big pot of drip coffee on weekdays so he can bring a thermos to work. But on weekends he, too, luxuriates in cappuccinos at home. I love that it takes no effort or brain space and it saves us so much money. We have a small apartment without a lot of counter space, so we got rid of our microwave to make space for this and I haven’t regretted it one bit.

I don’t drink coffee, but I’m a prolific tea drinker. I recently discovered Brooklyn-based tea brand Dona when I stopped by my local Variety Coffee and immediately fell in love with its high-quality, sustainable tea blends. I’ve been making my way through this Tea Library set (which, by the way, would make a very nice gift for a tea lover); it contains the brand’s entire menu of green, white, oolong, black, and herbal teas, and you really can tell that these blends have been carefully and thoughtfully crafted. Every morning, the first thing I do after waking up is turn on my Stagg Fellow kettle, which boils water in two minutes; my trick is to pour the hot water into my Hydro Flask before dropping in a tea bag, which makes replenishing my mug very easy and convenient.

We are coffee people. Nothing too fancy, because, while I would love to drink espresso at home, I am generally anti-pod-machine and overwhelmed by the potential learning curve (and expense) of getting started. Maybe I’ll be inspired by whatever lattes or other drinks my fellow Strategist folks are making!

Amazon tells me I have purchased this two times, the last time in April 2022, which was apparently when I broke the first one.

I literally just bought a 1,000-pack, which should be about a year’s supply for two of us typically drinking one pour-over per day with an occasional afternoon second cup.

Our “backup” method, or what we use when we are making more coffee than just the two individual pour-overs, is a classic Bodum French Press.

We also have an AeroPress that we use occasionally. If we host a larger group, I’ll borrow a bigger drip coffee maker from my parents.

I have this in all black. I love the look of the ones they have now with a walnut handle, but I’ll wait to replace until the current one fails. We’ve had ours since Christmas 2018.

I need to check how long we’ve had this one, at least since 2018 as well.

I bought this because the price was right. It works fine, but I don’t love how the auto-shut-off has never been quite what I expect or want it to be. Maybe I’ll replace or upgrade at some point, but there is really no need at the moment.

My mug is always my beloved Ember. I’m currently testing the new Ember 3 and its new tumbler! My husband uses a Fellow Carter (though his is a branded one from Grand Coffee in San Francisco that’s no longer available).

We brew two single pour-overs every morning — one dripper, used twice, and freshly weighed and ground beans. Once we open a bag of beans, we store it in a jar I got from the original Stumptown in Portland about 20 years ago, brown glass, no vacuum seal or anything — it’s good enough! I love to get “fancy” beans occasionally as a treat, but our go-to daily is Counter Culture Coffee Apollo Blend. I swear, coffee has gotten so expensive. I shop around and buy multiple bags at a time from Whole Foods or Target when it goes on sale. I also like a variety of “upgrade” beans from Grand in San Francisco, Four Barrel in San Francisco, Stumptown, Blue Bottle, Rising Star (a Cleveland roaster), and Troubadour (another Cleveland roaster).
